provenance.rightsNote: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of Machiavelli's The Prince, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (Marriott 1908; Thomson 1882) and checked against the Italian; modern translations consulted, not quoted. In progress, chapter by chapter.
sourcesCited: Italian, the original text of Il Principe
W. K. Marriott, The Prince (1908, public domain)

character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: The Lectio Edition renders Machiavelli's The Prince in plain modern English that keeps its cold clarity and bite — how power is won, held, and lost; fortune and virtù; cruelty and mercy weighed as instruments — without the antique stiffness.
introduction: The Prince is a short, shocking handbook on power, written by an out-of-work diplomat hoping to win back a place in Medici Florence. It sets aside how rulers ought to behave for how they actually must, if they mean to keep their state. Bracing, unsentimental, and still argued over five centuries later.

divergences.phrase: o per fortuna o per virtù
divergences.older: "by fortune or by ability" (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: "by luck or by skill"
divergences.note: Two of Machiavelli's signature terms enter here. Fortuna is the run of chance and circumstance outside a man's control; virtù is not Christian "virtue" but force of character — skill, drive, nerve, the capacity to act and impose one's will. Throughout this edition we render fortuna by its sense (fortune, luck, chance) and virtù as skill, prowess, or force of character as the context demands, never as moral "virtue." Here the crisp pairing "luck or skill" preserves the antithesis Machiavelli builds the whole book on.

divergences.phrase: stati / dominii
divergences.older: "states ... powers" (Marriott)
divergences.lectio: "state ... power"
divergences.note: Stato is the other load-bearing term: the prince's hold on rule, his apparatus of power, not the modern abstract "State." We keep "state" where it reads naturally and reach for "power" or "rule" where the sense is dominion held over men, so the word stays concrete throughout.

divergences.phrase: For the hereditary prince has less reason and less need to give offense, and so he is the more loved
divergences.older: For the hereditary prince has less cause and less necessity to offend; hence it happens that he will be more loved (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: has less reason and less need to give offense, and so he is the more loved
divergences.note: The Italian 'ha meno cagione e meno necessità di offendere' turns on 'offendere' — to wrong, harm, or antagonize subjects, not merely to insult. Rendered 'give offense' to keep the active sense: the settled prince has fewer occasions to injure his people, and is loved for it. This is Machiavelli's structural point, not a sentiment — security breeds restraint, and restraint breeds affection.

divergences.phrase: one upheaval always leaves behind the toothing on which the next is built
divergences.older: one change always leaves the toothing for another (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: one upheaval always leaves behind the toothing on which the next is built
divergences.note: Italian 'una mutazione lascia sempre lo addentellato per la edificazione dell'altra.' 'Addentellato' is a mason's term: the projecting stones left at the edge of a wall so a later wall can be keyed onto them. 'Toothing' is the exact English building term, kept here; the gloss 'on which the next is built' unpacks 'per la edificazione' so the metaphor lands for a modern reader without diluting it.

divergences.phrase: a man of merely ordinary ability can keep his footing
divergences.older: for a prince of average powers to maintain himself in his state (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: a man of merely ordinary ability can keep his footing
divergences.note: Italian 'uno principe di ordinaria industria.' 'Industria' here means practical skill and diligence — a near neighbor of 'virtù' but lower-key, the workmanlike competence of getting on. Translated 'ordinary ability' rather than 'average powers' to mark that Machiavelli is deliberately setting the bar low: holding an inherited state takes no exceptional 'virtù,' only not fumbling the inheritance.

divergences.phrase: men ought either to be caressed or crushed
divergences.older: men ought either to be well treated or crushed (Marriott, 1908)
divergences.lectio: men ought either to be caressed or crushed
divergences.note: Machiavelli's Italian is "gli uomini si debbono o vezzeggiare o spegnere" — literally to caress/cosset or to snuff out. Marriott's "well treated" softens the first half into mere good government; we keep "caressed" to preserve the deliberate cruelty of the pairing — a man is either pampered into harmlessness or annihilated, with nothing in between. "Spegnere" (to extinguish) is rendered "crushed" by tradition; the bleaner word keeps the bite.

divergences.phrase: war is never avoided, only postponed to another man's advantage
divergences.older: war is not to be avoided, but is only to be put off to the advantage of others (Marriott, 1908)
divergences.lectio: war is never avoided, only postponed to another man's advantage
divergences.note: The Italian is "la guerra non si lieva, ma si differisce con vantaggio d'altri." "Si lieva" means lifted or removed, not merely sidestepped; war cannot be cancelled, only deferred — and deferral always pays off for the other side, never for you. We sharpen Marriott's looser phrasing so the maxim lands as the cold rule of timing it is.

divergences.locus: throughout — qualities of rulers and states
divergences.phrase: skill / foresight (virtù)
divergences.older: great energy / valour / virtue (Marriott, 1908)
divergences.lectio: skill, prowess, foresight — translated by context, never as moral "virtue"
divergences.note: Machiavelli's "virtù" (as in "buona fortuna e gran virtù") is not moral virtue but effective capacity: skill, drive, command of one's craft and one's circumstances. Marriott swings between "energy" and "valour"; we render it by context ("great skill," "their own skill and foresight") and flag it here, since reading it as English "virtue" inverts Machiavelli's whole argument. Likewise "fortuna" we keep as fortune/luck and "stato" as state/territory, as the sense requires.

divergences.phrase: servi e mancipii
divergences.older: "slaves and bondmen" (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: "slaves and bondmen"
divergences.note: Machiavelli's Italian is "sendo tutti stiavi e obligati," with the ministers earlier called "servi" who serve "per grazia e concessione sua" — by the prince's favor and leave. The point is not chattel slavery but total dependence: every officer of the Turk's state holds his place at the prince's pleasure, owns nothing of his own, and so has nothing to bargain with and no following to deliver. We keep the traditional "slaves and bondmen" for its bluntness, since the whole contrast with France's hereditary barons rests on it — bound men cannot be bought, because they have no independent base to sell.

divergences.phrase: antichità di sangue
divergences.older: "antiquity of blood" (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: "antiquity of blood"
divergences.note: The French lords hold their rank "non per grazia del Signore, ma per antichità di sangue" — not by the prince's grant but by the age of their lineage. This is the structural hinge of the chapter: power that descends by blood cannot be revoked, so it creates rival centers of loyalty the king cannot dissolve. We render it literally rather than as "ancient nobility," because Machiavelli is naming the mechanism — inherited blood, not royal favor — that makes France easy to invade and hard to keep.

divergences.phrase: dalla disformità del suggetto
divergences.older: "by the want of uniformity in the subject state" (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: "on the difference in the states he takes"
divergences.note: The closing antithesis is "non da poca o assai virtù del vincitore, ma dalla disformità del suggetto" — not from the conqueror's having little or much virtù, but from the disformità of the suggetto, the thing conquered. Marriott's "want of uniformity in the subject state" is accurate but stiff. We keep virtù as skill (per this edition's settled rendering) and turn the abstract "disformità del suggetto" into the plain "the difference in the states he takes," so the cold final verdict lands: outcomes depend on the structure of what you seize, not on your own brilliance.

divergences.phrase: el nome della libertà e gli ordini antiqui sua
divergences.older: the watchword of liberty and its ancient privileges as a rallying point (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the name of liberty and its ancient privileges
divergences.note: This is the cold heart of the chapter. The Italian 'sempre ha per refugio nella rebellione el nome della libertà e gli ordini antiqui sua' makes liberty a thing a free city reaches for — a 'refugio,' a rallying-point — every time it revolts. Marriott's 'watchword' is vivid but adds a metaphor not in the Italian; we keep the plainer 'the name of liberty,' since Machiavelli's force lies precisely in the bare word 'name': not the thing itself but the name of it, invoked, is enough to set men in arms. The point is preserved undiluted — a free city carries this fuse inside it forever.

divergences.phrase: le disfecero ... disfaccia ... disfatto
divergences.older: dismantled them ... does not destroy it ... be destroyed by it (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: dismantled them ... and does not destroy it ... may expect to be destroyed by it
divergences.note: Machiavelli rings the single verb 'disfare' — to undo, unmake, take apart — across the whole passage: Rome 'le disfecero,' the new master who 'non la disfaccia' will 'essere disfatto da quella.' Marriott reaches for 'dismantled' / 'ruin' / 'destroy,' losing the grim repetition. We keep 'dismantled' for cities physically pulled down and 'destroy' for the man, so the chapter's chilling symmetry survives — you unmake the free city, or it unmakes you.

divergences.phrase: maggiore vita, maggiore odio, più desiderio di vendetta
divergences.older: more vitality, greater hatred, and more desire for vengeance (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: more life, more hatred, more hunger for revenge
divergences.note: The Italian piles up three nouns in flat parallel — 'più vita, maggiore odio, più desiderio di vendetta' — and the rhythm is the argument: a republic is more alive, and that aliveness is dangerous. Marriott's 'vitality' is a touch clinical; we keep the blunt 'life,' and render 'desiderio di vendetta' as 'hunger for revenge' to give the line the heat Machiavelli loads into it. Nothing is added — the menace is already in the original.

divergences.phrase: all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed
divergences.older: all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed
divergences.note: The Italian is 'Di qui nacque che tutti li profeti armati vinsono, e li disarmati ruinorno.' This is the chapter's hammer-blow, and we keep it word for word with the tradition — no softening. 'Vinsono' is flatly 'conquered, won'; 'ruinorno' is 'were ruined, came to ruin, were destroyed.' The line yokes Moses and Romulus to brute force and casts religious mission as a question of arms; nothing in 'prophet' is allowed to spiritualize it. The reader should feel the cold equation: faith without the power to compel does not survive.

divergences.phrase: owed nothing to luck except the opportunity ... the raw material they could then mold
divergences.older: they owed anything to fortune beyond opportunity, which brought them the material to mould into the form which seemed best to them (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: owed nothing to luck except the opportunity, which handed them the raw material they could then mold into whatever shape they pleased
divergences.note: Here Machiavelli draws the exact line between 'fortuna' and 'virtù' that the whole chapter turns on. Fortune's entire contribution is the 'occasione' — the opening, the material conditions (an enslaved people, a scattered city); everything done with that opening is 'virtù,' rendered here by its sense as force of mind and skill, never moral virtue. We keep 'mold ... raw material' to preserve the sculptor's image: chance supplies only the clay, the man supplies the form. The closing antithesis — 'without that opportunity their force of mind would have been wasted; without that force the opportunity would have come in vain' — is balanced to match the Italian's symmetry.

divergences.phrase: whether to carry their work through they must beg, or whether they can compel
divergences.older: whether, to consummate their enterprise, have they to use prayers or can they use force (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: whether to carry their work through they must beg, or whether they can compel
divergences.note: The Italian is 'se per condurre l'opera loro hanno bisogno di pregare, ovvero possono forzare.' Marriott's 'use prayers' is literal for 'pregare' but misleads a modern ear toward religious prayer; the sense is entreaty — having to ask, persuade, depend on others' consent — set against 'forzare,' to compel by force. We render it 'beg ... compel' to keep the stark binary that sets up the armed/unarmed prophets verdict in the next breath: the innovator who can only ask is finished; the one who can force endures.

divergences.phrase: lo fece mettere una mattina a Cesena in dua pezzi ... rimasono quelli populi in un tempo satisfatti e stupidi
divergences.older: one morning caused him to be executed and left on the piazza at Cesena with the block and a bloody knife at his side ... caused the people to be at once satisfied and dismayed (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: one morning he had Remirro laid out in the piazza at Cesena in two pieces, with a block of wood and a bloody knife beside him. The ferocity of that spectacle left the people at once satisfied and stupefied
divergences.note: This is the chapter's cold climax, and Marriott blunts it twice. 'In dua pezzi' is literally 'in two pieces' — the body cut in two and displayed; Marriott's vague 'executed and left' loses the butchery, so we restore it. More important is the last word: Machiavelli's 'satisfatti e stupidi' is 'satisfied and stupefied' — stunned, struck dumb. Marriott softens 'stupidi' to 'dismayed,' which adds disapproval the Italian does not have. The horror of the people is not moral dismay but blank shock; they got the cruelty's author handed to them (satisfied) and were paralyzed by the violence of it (stupefied). We keep both halves bare, since the whole lesson — punish through a minister, then punish the minister — depends on that double effect landing exactly.

divergences.phrase: le armi e fortuna d'altri
divergences.older: the arms and fortunes of others ... by the arms of others or by good fortune (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the arms and fortune of others ... by the arms of others or by fortune
divergences.note: The chapter's title and spine turn on the pairing of borrowed 'armi' (arms, the force of others) and 'fortuna' (luck, the favor of others). Per this edition's settled rendering, 'fortuna' stays 'fortune' or 'luck' — never moral 'good fortune' as a blessing, but the run of chance and another man's favor, the most 'inconstant and unstable' thing there is. Borgia is the test case: everything he built rested on his father's fortune, and when that fortune turned (the pope's death, his own illness), the structure fell. We keep 'arms and fortune of others' flat and repeated, because Machiavelli rings it like a refrain — the man who rises on what others lend him holds nothing of his own.

divergences.phrase: la estraordinaria ed estrema malignità di fortuna
divergences.older: the extraordinary and extreme malignity of fortune (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the extraordinary and extreme malignity of fortune
divergences.note: Here Machiavelli renders his final verdict on Cesare Borgia, and we keep it word for word with the tradition. 'Malignità di fortuna' is fortune's active ill-will — not mere bad luck but luck turned malignant, almost personified, a force that singles a man out. This is the cold heart of Borgia's case: he did everything a wise and able man should do (he is offered as the model new prince), and was undone not by any flaw in his skill ('virtù') but by fortune's freak cruelty — his own near-fatal illness striking at the very moment his father died. We preserve the full doubled intensifier, 'extraordinary and extreme,' because Machiavelli is straining to insist the failure was unrepeatable, so that the model still stands.

divergences.phrase: ma non gloria
divergences.older: such methods may gain empire, but not glory (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: Such methods may win you power, but not glory.
divergences.note: The cold hinge of the chapter. The Italian is 'Non si può ancora chiamare virtù ammazzare li sua cittadini, tradire li amici, essere sanza fede, sanza pietà, sanza religione; li quali modi possono fare acquistare imperio, ma non gloria.' We keep virtù as 'skill' (this edition's settled rendering) rather than Marriott's 'talent,' so the chapter's argument holds: butchery and treachery can buy a man dominion but never honor — they are outside the order of virtù altogether. 'Imperio' is rendered 'power' to stay concrete; 'gloria' is left bare as 'glory,' the thing crime can never reach.

divergences.phrase: crudeltà male usate o bene usate
divergences.older: severities being badly or properly used (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: whether cruelty is badly or well used
divergences.note: Marriott, following Burd, softens 'crudeltà' to 'severities'; we restore the blunt word Machiavelli wrote — cruelty. The Italian distinguishes cruelties 'bene usate' (well used) from 'male usate' (badly used): well used are 'quelle che si fanno a uno tratto, per la necessità dello assicurarsi, e di poi non vi si insiste drento, ma si convertono in più utilità de' sudditi che si può' — done at a single stroke for self-security, then stopped and turned to the subjects' good. Badly used are those that, 'ancora che nel principio sieno poche, più tosto col tempo crescono che le si spenghino' — few at first but multiplying with time. The whole grim calculus depends on keeping the word 'cruelty,' not laundering it.

divergences.phrase: le iniurie si debbono fare tutte insieme ... benefizii a poco a poco
divergences.older: injuries ought to be done all at one time ... benefits ought to be given little by little (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: injuries should be done all at once ... benefits should be handed out little by little
divergences.note: The most quoted line in the chapter, and we hold it exactly to the Italian: 'le iniurie si debbono fare tutte insieme, acciò che, assaporandosi meno, offendino meno; e' benefizii si debbono fare a poco a poco, acciò che si assaporino meglio.' The verb is 'assaporare' — to taste, to savor — and Machiavelli runs it both ways: harm crammed into one mouthful is tasted less and so wounds less; kindness doled out in sips is savored longer. We keep the eating metaphor ('tasted,' 'flavor') intact, since the cold symmetry of the maxim is the whole point — never blunt one half, never soften the other.

divergences.phrase: el populo non vuole essere comandato né oppresso da' grandi, e li grandi vogliono comandare e opprimere el populo
divergences.older: the people do not wish to be ruled nor oppressed by the nobles, and the nobles wish to rule and oppress the people (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the people do not want to be commanded or oppressed by the nobles, and the nobles want to command and oppress the people
divergences.note: This is the engine of the whole chapter — Machiavelli's two 'umori,' the two clashing appetites that exist in every city. We keep 'comandare/comandato' as 'command/commanded' rather than the looser 'rule,' because the verb is concrete and active: the nobles' desire is to give orders and grind men down, the people's only to escape being ground down. The flat parallel of the two clauses is the argument, and nothing is added or softened: the people's aim is merely defensive ('not to be oppressed'), the nobles' aggressive, and on that asymmetry rests Machiavelli's later verdict that the people's cause is 'more honest.'

divergences.phrase: chi fonda in sul populo, fonda in sul fango
divergences.older: He who builds on the people, builds on the mud (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: he who builds on the people builds on mud
divergences.note: The famous proverb — and the point is that it is NOT Machiavelli's view but the 'proverbio trito,' the worn-out commonplace he quotes only to qualify it. We keep the blunt 'builds on mud' and, crucially, preserve his correction intact: the proverb holds only for a 'cittadino privato,' a private citizen who founds on the people and fools himself that they will rescue him when his enemies or the magistrates close in — and is duly deceived, as the Gracchi and Giorgio Scali were. A prince who can command, who has nerve, and who keeps the people needing him will not be deceived. The argument's whole force lies in this hinge, so we render it so the reader feels Machiavelli turning the proverb against the men who use it.

divergences.locus: paragraph 3 (nobles vs. people, the danger weighed)
divergences.phrase: el peggio che possa aspettare uno principe dal populo inimico è l'essere abbandonato da lui; ma da' grandi inimici non solo debbe temere di essere abbandonato, ma etiam che loro li venghino contro
divergences.older: The worst that a prince may expect from a hostile people is to be abandoned by them; but from hostile nobles he has not only to fear abandonment, but also that they will rise against him (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: The worst a prince has to fear from a hostile people is to be abandoned by them; but from hostile nobles he has to fear not only abandonment but their turning against him
divergences.note: The cold asymmetry that justifies leaning on the people, not the nobles. A hostile people is a passive danger — at worst it walks away ('abbandonato'); hostile nobles are an active one — they 'li venghino contro,' come at him, take the field against him. We keep both halves sharp and unsoftened, and carry through Machiavelli's reasoning: the nobles are 'più antiveggenti e astuti,' shrewder and more far-sighted, so they move early to save themselves and court whoever they think will win. That treachery, not mere desertion, is why a prince stands less securely when the nobles raise him than when the people do.

divergences.phrase: la natura delli uomini è così obligarsi per li benefizii che si fanno, come per quelli che si ricevano
divergences.older: it is the nature of men to be bound by the benefits they confer as much as by those they receive (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: it is the nature of men to feel as much bound by the good they do as by the good they receive
divergences.note: The quiet psychological hinge of the chapter. Machiavelli's point is counter-intuitive and easily missed: men are tied to you not only by the kindnesses they get but by the sacrifices they make on your behalf. Having burned their own houses in the prince's defense, the people are now invested in him and cling tighter — the cost they have paid binds them. We keep the symmetry of 'fanno / ricevano' (do / receive) flat and bare, since the whole consolation Machiavelli offers the besieged prince rests on it; nothing is added, only the stiff 'confer' is plained to 'do.'

divergences.phrase: Le città della Magna sono liberissime
divergences.older: The cities of Germany are absolutely free (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: The cities of Germany are wholly free
divergences.note: 'Magna' is Machiavelli's name for the German lands of the Empire, and the free imperial cities are his model of a principality that needs no one: walled, gunned, stocked with a year's food, and run so that the common people always have paid work. We keep 'Germany' (Marriott's settled rendering) and translate 'liberissime' as 'wholly free' rather than the looser 'absolutely free,' to mark that their freedom is concrete and structural — they obey the emperor only 'quando le vogliono,' when they choose to — not a sentiment but a fact of their walls and stores.

divergences.phrase: difendersi dentro alle mura
divergences.older: are forced to defend themselves by sheltering behind walls (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: are forced to shelter behind their walls and defend those
divergences.note: The chapter's whole taxonomy turns on this one line: a prince either can 'fare una giornata' — give battle in the open — or he cannot, and must hole up behind his walls. Marriott's phrasing is accurate; we sharpen the contrast with the preceding clause ('face the enemy in the open') so the binary lands cleanly, since everything that follows — the advice to fortify the town and never defend the open country — flows from which side of this line a prince falls on. 'Defend those' keeps Machiavelli's pointed sense that such a prince defends the walls, not the country.

divergences.phrase: sendo esaltati e mantenuti da Dio, sarebbe offizio di uomo presuntuoso e temerario discorrerne
divergences.older: being exalted and maintained by God, it would be the act of a presumptuous and rash man to discuss them (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: being exalted and maintained by God, it would be the act of a presumptuous and rash man to discuss them
divergences.note: The most charged line in the chapter, and we hold it word for word with the tradition. Machiavelli has just catalogued the absurd security of Church states — princes who do not defend, subjects who are not governed — and then, at the one point where a writer might explain the mechanism, he stops: these powers are beyond the reach of the human mind, so to analyze them would be 'presuntuoso e temerario,' presumptuous and rash. The irony is left entirely intact and unmarked, exactly as in the Italian: the man who anatomizes every other kind of rule with cold nerve here professes a piety that reads as its opposite. Softening or explaining it would kill it; the restraint is the joke, and the joke is the argument.

divergences.phrase: hanno stati e non li difendono; hanno sudditi e non li governano
divergences.older: These princes alone have states and do not defend them; and they have subjects and do not rule them (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: These princes alone have states and do not defend them; they have subjects and do not govern them
divergences.note: Machiavelli builds the paradox in flat parallel clauses, and the rhythm is the point: have states / do not defend, have subjects / do not govern, undefended / not taken, ungoverned / do not mind. Every other chapter of the book is about how brutally hard it is to defend a state and govern subjects; here is the one kind of principality where neither labor is needed, and the deadpan symmetry exposes how strange — almost comic — that exemption is. We keep 'govern' rather than Marriott's 'rule' for 'governano,' to mark the concrete activity of governing that these princes simply skip, and hold the clauses bare and balanced so the absurdity lands without comment.

divergences.locus: paragraph 4 (the temporal growth of the Church)
divergences.phrase: benché la intenzione sua non fussi di fare grande la Chiesa, ma il duca, nondimanco ciò che e' fece tornò a grandezza della Chiesa
divergences.older: although his intention was not to aggrandize the Church, but the duke, nevertheless what he did contributed to the greatness of the Church (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: although his aim was not to make the Church great but the duke, what he did told all the same to the Church's greatness
divergences.note: This is the quiet, devastating hinge of the chapter's history. Alexander VI is being praised — he 'showed how far a pope could prevail with money and with arms' — but Machiavelli immediately notes that the pope was working not for the Church at all but for his own son, Cesare Borgia (Duke Valentino), and that the Church grew great only as a by-product, 'falling heir' to Borgia's ruin. We keep the concessive structure ('although ... what he did told all the same') tight, so the reader feels the cold mechanism beneath the pious surface: the temporal greatness of the Church was the accidental residue of a father's dynastic scheming. The verb 'tornò a grandezza' — turned to, redounded to greatness — is rendered 'told all the same to the Church's greatness' to keep that sense of unintended outcome rather than deliberate design.

divergences.phrase: le buone leggi e le buone armi
divergences.older: good laws and good arms (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: good laws and good arms
divergences.note: The chapter's load-bearing maxim, kept word for word with the tradition. The Italian is 'I principali fondamenti che abbino tutti li stati, così nuovi come vecchi o misti, sono le buone legge e le buone arme; e perché non può essere buone legge dove non sono buone arme, e dove sono buone arme conviene siano buone legge.' The whole argument hinges on the order of cause: arms come first, and good laws follow only where there are good arms, never the reverse. We hold 'good laws and good arms' flat and unsoftened, since Machiavelli is overturning the pious commonplace that law founds a state — for him it is force that founds it, and law that rests on force.

divergences.phrase: inutili e periculose ... disunite, ambiziose, sanza disciplina, infedeli
divergences.older: useless and dangerous ... disunited, ambitious, and without discipline, unfaithful, valiant before friends, cowardly before enemies (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: useless and dangerous ... disunited, ambitious, undisciplined, and faithless; brave among friends, cowardly among enemies
divergences.note: The famous denunciation of mercenaries, and we keep the hammering parallel intact. The Italian is 'le armi mercennarie e ausiliarie sono inutili e periculose ... perché le sono disunite, ambiziose, sanza disciplina, infideli; gagliarde fra gli amici, fra' nimici vile.' Each adjective lands as its own blow, and the sting is in the antithesis 'gagliarde fra gli amici, fra' nimici vile' — swaggering among allies, gutless against the foe. We render 'gagliarde' as 'brave' and 'vile' as 'cowardly' to keep the bare contempt; nothing is added and nothing softened, because the indictment is built to accelerate.

divergences.phrase: aspirano alla loro propria grandezza
divergences.older: they always aspire to their own greatness (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: they will always be reaching for their own greatness
divergences.note: The cold core of the case against mercenary captains. Machiavelli sets a trap with no exit: 'O sono uomini valenti, o no; se sono, non te ne puoi fidare, perché sempre aspireranno alla grandezza propria.' The able captain cannot be trusted precisely because he is able — his skill is a threat, since it serves his own ambition, by 'oppressing you, who are their master' or by moving against others against your will; the inept one simply ruins you outright. We keep 'reaching for their own greatness' to mark the verb as an unbroken drive, not a single act: the talent that makes a hired commander useful is the very thing that makes him deadly to the man who hires him.

divergences.phrase: perdendo rimani disfatto, vincendo resti loro prigione
divergences.older: for losing, one is undone, and winning, one is their captive (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: For if you lose, you are undone; and if you win, you are their prisoner.
divergences.note: The cold heart of the chapter, and we hold it tight to the Italian: 'perchè perdendo rimani disfatto, vincendo resti loro prigione.' The trap is sprung in a single balanced line — defeat ruins you, victory delivers you. 'Disfatto' is Machiavelli's recurring verb of unmaking (rendered 'undone' here, as elsewhere in this edition), and 'prigione' is flatly 'prisoner,' not the softer 'captive': borrowed arms that win the field own the man who borrowed them. We keep the second-person 'you' to make the threat land on the reader, and refuse to blunt either half — the whole case against auxiliaries is that they are more dangerous than mercenaries precisely because there is no good outcome.

divergences.phrase: nei mercennarii è più pericolosa la ignavia, nelli ausiliarii la virtù
divergences.older: in mercenaries dastardy is most dangerous; in auxiliaries, valour (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: with mercenaries the danger is their cowardice; with auxiliaries, their courage
divergences.note: A sharp paradox that turns on this edition's settled rendering of 'virtù.' Machiavelli sets 'ignavia' (cowardice, sloth) against 'virtù' — here not moral virtue and not even skill, but the dangerous effectiveness of a force that is good at war but obeys someone other than you. The mercenary's vice is that he is useless; the auxiliary's menace is that he is useful — disciplined, united, and loyal to his own master. We render 'virtù' as 'courage' to keep the antithesis with 'cowardice' clean, since the whole point is that the auxiliary's strength, not his weakness, is what undoes you. Marriott's 'dastardy/valour' is accurate but stiff; we plain it without losing the cold symmetry.

divergences.phrase: o le ti caggiono di dosso, o le ti pesano, o le ti stringono
divergences.older: the arms of others either fall from your back, or they weigh you down, or they bind you fast (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: In short, another man's armor either slips off your back, or weighs you down, or binds you fast.
divergences.note: The chapter's one biblical figure, and its image for borrowed arms entire. The Italian rings three verbs in flat parallel — 'caggiono di dosso' (fall off the back), 'pesano' (weigh down), 'stringono' (constrict, bind tight) — and the rhythm is the argument: armor that is not your own can only fail you in one of three ways. We keep all three blows bare and in order, rendering 'caggiono di dosso' as 'slips off your back' for the body's sake and 'stringono' as 'binds you fast' to preserve the menace of the last beat. David meets Goliath with his own sling and knife; the lesson is that a prince must fight in arms fitted to himself, never in another power's.

divergences.phrase: non avere altro obietto né altro pensiero, né prendere cosa alcuna per sua arte, fuora della guerra
divergences.older: ought to have no other aim or thought, nor select anything else for his study, than war and its rules and discipline (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: should have no other aim or thought, nor take up anything else for his study, but war and its organization and discipline
divergences.note: The hammer-blow that opens and governs the whole chapter, and we keep it bare and absolute. The Italian — 'non avere altro obietto né altro pensiero, né prendere cosa alcuna per sua arte, fuora della guerra' — admits no second interest: war is not merely the prince's chief art but his only one ('la sola arte che si aspetta a chi comanda'). The doubled negation 'altro obietto né altro pensiero' is held flat as 'no other aim or thought,' and 'fuora della guerra' as the exclusive 'but war,' so the reader feels the totality. Nothing is softened toward a more reasonable 'war should be his main concern'; Machiavelli means it should be the whole of it.

divergences.phrase: stare sempre in sulle caccie ... imparare la natura de' siti, e cognoscere come sorgono i monti, come imboccano le valli, come giacciono i piani
divergences.older: to follow incessantly the chase, by which he accustoms his body to hardships, and learns something of the nature of localities, and gets to find out how the mountains rise, how the valleys open out, how the plains lie (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: never stop hunting, by which he hardens his body to hardship and at the same time learns the lie of the land — how the mountains rise, how the valleys open out, how the plains lie
divergences.note: Hunting here is not sport but military reconnaissance: Machiavelli makes it the practical method by which a prince in peacetime trains his body ('assuefà il corpo a' disagi') and reads terrain as a commander must. We keep the concrete physical verbs — mountains 'sorgono' (rise), valleys 'imboccano' (open out, run in), plains 'giacciono' (lie) — rather than abstracting them, because the whole point is that the prince acquires a soldier's eye for ground. 'Hardens his body to hardship' holds the deliberate harshness of 'assuefà ... a' disagi' against Marriott's softer 'accustoms.'

divergences.locus: paragraph 4 (the closing on imitation and fortune)
divergences.phrase: Alessandro Magno imitava Achille, Cesare Alessandro, Scipione Ciro ... per potersene valere nelle avversità
divergences.older: Alexander the Great imitated Achilles, Caesar Alexander, Scipio Cyrus ... so that they may be available to him in adversity, so that if fortune chances it may find him prepared to resist her blows (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: Alexander the Great imitated Achilles, Caesar imitated Alexander, and Scipio imitated Cyrus ... so that he may draw on it in adversity — so that when fortune turns, it finds him ready to withstand her
divergences.note: The chapter ends by binding the reading of histories to its cold purpose. The chain of imitation (Alexander/Achilles, Caesar/Alexander, Scipio/Cyrus) is preserved whole, with Cyrus reached specifically through Xenophon's life of him — Machiavelli's pointed source. The close, 'mai ne' tempi pacifici stare ozioso, ma con industria farne capitale, per potersene valere nelle avversità,' carries this edition's settled rendering of fortuna: not a personified goddess to be piously feared, but the run of chance that turns against a man. We keep 'farne capitale' as 'make capital of them' — the prince banks his peacetime study like a reserve — and render the final clause as fortune turning so it 'finds him ready to withstand her,' matching the readiness-against-reversal that the whole book turns on.

divergences.phrase: andare dietro alla verità effettuale della cosa
divergences.older: to follow up the real truth of the matter than the imagination of it (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: to go after the effectual truth of the matter than the imagination of it
divergences.note: This is the most famous phrase in the book and the hinge of Machiavelli's whole method, so we restore his coined term rather than smooth it away. 'Verità effettuale' is not just the 'real' truth but the effective, operative truth — what actually works and actually happens, as opposed to 'l'immaginazione di essa,' how men imagine or wish things to be. Marriott's 'real truth' is accurate but loses the manufactured, almost technical strangeness of 'effettuale.' We keep 'effectual truth,' the rendering the tradition has settled on, because Machiavelli is announcing a new way of reasoning about politics — from results, not from ideals — and the odd word is the announcement.

divergences.phrase: egli è tanto discosto da come si vive, a come si doveria vivere ... impara piuttosto la rovina, che la preservazione sua
divergences.older: how one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live, that he who neglects what is done for what ought to be done, sooner effects his ruin than his preservation (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: how one lives is so far removed from how one ought to live, that the man who lets go of what is done for what ought to be done sooner learns his ruin than his preservation
divergences.note: The cold heart of the chapter, and we hold it tight to the Italian. 'Come si vive' against 'come si doveria vivere' — how one lives versus how one ought to live — is the bare antithesis the whole argument rests on, and nothing is allowed to soften it. The verb is 'impara,' learns: the man who abandons the real for the ideal 'impara piuttosto la rovina,' learns ruin rather than preservation — as if ruin were the lesson such idealism teaches. Marriott's 'effects his ruin' is smoother but loses 'impara'; we keep 'learns his ruin' to preserve Machiavelli's grim irony, that following the moralists' rule schools a prince in his own destruction. 'Discosto' is rendered 'removed' to keep the sense of distance between two whole ways of being.

divergences.phrase: imparare a potere essere non buono, ed usarlo e non usarlo secondo la necessità
divergences.older: to know how to do wrong, and to make use of it or not according to necessity (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: learn how not to be good, and to use this or not use it according to necessity
divergences.note: Machiavelli's most quoted command, and Marriott blunts it. The Italian is 'imparare a potere essere non buono' — to learn how to be able not to be good — not 'to do wrong.' The difference is the whole point: Machiavelli is not telling the prince to be evil but to acquire a capacity, the freedom to set goodness aside when necessity demands and to take it up again when it does not. 'Non buono' is the careful negation of the moralists' 'buono'; we keep 'not to be good' bare, since the chilling restraint of the phrase — a learned ability, used or withheld 'secondo la necessità,' by the calculus of need — is exactly what makes it shocking. To translate it as 'do wrong' moralizes the very neutrality Machiavelli is at pains to construct.

divergences.phrase: qualche cosa che parrà virtù ... la rovina sua; e qualcun'altra che parrà vizio ... la sicurtà ed il ben essere suo
divergences.older: something which looks like virtue, if followed, would be his ruin; whilst something else, which looks like vice, yet followed brings him security and prosperity (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: something will be found that looks like virtue, and following it would be his ruin, while something else that looks like vice, followed, brings him security and well-being
divergences.note: The chapter's final blow, and the payoff of the 'effectual truth.' Machiavelli twists the two key words against themselves: a thing 'che parrà virtù' — that will look like virtue — leads to 'rovina,' ruin; and a thing 'che parrà vizio,' that will look like vice, brings 'sicurtà ed il ben essere,' security and well-being. The verb is 'parrà,' will seem — appearance set against effect, which is the whole method of the book in one sentence. We keep 'looks like virtue / looks like vice' to preserve that gap between seeming and outcome, and render 'ben essere' as 'well-being' rather than Marriott's 'prosperity,' since Machiavelli means the prince's whole secure flourishing, not merely his wealth. Nothing is softened: the cold lesson is that the names good and evil do not track the results, and a prince must reckon by results.

divergences.phrase: non è cosa che consumi sé stessa quanto la liberalità
divergences.older: there is nothing wastes so rapidly as liberality (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: there is nothing that consumes itself like generosity
divergences.note: The chapter's hammer-line, and we hold it to the Italian: 'non è cosa che consumi sé stessa quanto la liberalità.' The verb is reflexive — 'consuma sé stessa,' consumes itself — and that self-cannibalizing image is the whole point: generosity is the one thing that, in the very act of being used, eats away the power to use it. Marriott's 'wastes so rapidly' keeps the speed but loses the reflexive bite; we restore 'consumes itself' so the paradox lands as Machiavelli built it. We also render 'liberalità' as 'generosity' rather than the antique 'liberality,' since the modern English word names exactly the open-handed spending he means, while 'liberality' has drifted toward political abstraction.

divergences.phrase: non si curare del nome del misero
divergences.older: he ought not to fear the reputation of being mean (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: he ought not to mind being called mean
divergences.note: Machiavelli's counsel is deliberately cold and counter-intuitive: a wise prince should positively accept the unflattering name. 'Il misero' is the miser, the stingy man — 'mean' in its older English sense of niggardly, kept here by the tradition for its bite. The point is not that meanness is good in itself but that it is the cheaper vice: it brings reproach but not hatred, and it leaves the prince solvent enough to defend himself and spare his people taxes. We keep 'mean' rather than modernizing to 'stingy,' since the chapter pivots on the bare opposition liberale / misero — generous versus mean — and the contempt in the word is part of the calculation the prince is told to swallow.

divergences.phrase: infamia sanza odio ... infamia con odio
divergences.older: reproach without hatred ... reproach with hatred (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: reproach without hatred ... reproach with hatred
divergences.note: The chapter ends on a balanced antithesis Machiavelli weighs like a ledger: 'una infamia sanza odio' against 'una infamia con odio.' Both courses cost the prince his good name — 'infamia' either way — so the choice is decided by the one thing that can actually unseat him: hatred. Meanness earns contempt but no hatred; the rapacity bred by failed generosity earns both. We keep the parallel flat and unsoftened, because the whole grim economy of the chapter resolves into this single weighing: a prince can survive being thought a miser, but not being hated, and so he should choose the reproach that comes without the hatred.

divergences.phrase: è molto più sicuro essere temuto che amato, quando si abbia a mancare dell'uno de' dua
divergences.older: it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: it is much safer to be feared than loved, if one of the two must be given up
divergences.note: The most quoted line in the book, and we hold it flat to the Italian, refusing every temptation to soften it. Machiavelli does not say a prince should prefer fear, but that fear is the safer of two goods a prince would ideally hold together — 'si abbia a mancare dell'uno de' dua,' if one of the two must be lacked. The whole cold calculus that follows depends on this conditional: love is a bond men cut whenever it pays ('rotto da ogni occasione di utilità propria'), while fear is held by 'timore di pena che non ti abbandona mai,' a dread of punishment that never deserts you. We keep 'feared than loved' bare and unhedged, since the chapter's force is precisely that it weighs affection as an instrument and finds it the weaker tool.

divergences.phrase: gli uomini sdimenticano più presto la morte del padre che la perdita del patrimonio
divergences.older: men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: men sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony
divergences.note: The chapter's bleakest aphorism, and we render it word for word with the tradition, since any softening would be a betrayal of its point. The verb 'sdimenticano' is flatly 'forget'; the shock is in the comparison Machiavelli draws without flinching — a man will get over his father's killing faster than over being robbed of his inheritance. We keep 'patrimony' rather than the looser 'property' here (though we use 'property' for 'roba' just above), because 'patrimonio' is specifically the estate handed down, the thing a man means to pass on, and the line cuts deepest when that exact sense is preserved. It is the cold ground of the whole counsel to be feared without being hated: shed blood if you must, with cause, but never touch what men own.

divergences.phrase: la sua inumana crudeltà
divergences.older: his inhuman cruelty (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: his inhuman cruelty
divergences.note: Machiavelli's example of cruelty put to perfect use, and we keep the blunt word he wrote — 'inumana crudeltà,' inhuman cruelty — without laundering it into 'severity' or 'sternness,' as is the temptation throughout this chapter. The point is deliberately scandalous: it was precisely this cruelty, joined to his 'virtù infinita' (rendered here as boundless prowess, per this edition's settled handling of virtù), that held a vast army of mixed races together through every reverse, where Scipio's praised leniency bred mutiny. We render 'virtù' as prowess, not 'valour' or 'virtue,' so the argument stands clear: cruelty is not the opposite of a commander's excellence but, well used, an indispensable part of it — and the 'short-sighted writers' who admire Hannibal's results while condemning their cause have simply failed to follow the logic.

divergences.phrase: la golpe e il lione
divergences.older: the fox and the lion (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the fox and the lion
divergences.note: The most famous image in the book, and we hold it word for word with the tradition. The Italian is 'debbe di quelle pigliare la golpe e il lione; perché il lione non si difende da' lacci, la golpe non si difende da' lupi.' The lesson is built on a precise crossing: each beast is helpless against exactly what the other masters — the lion's strength is blind to the trap ('lacci,' snares), the fox's cunning is defenseless against the wolf's force. So the prince needs both, 'fox to recognize the traps, lion to frighten off the wolves.' We keep the bare animal nouns and the chiasmus intact, since the whole argument that force and craft are inseparable rests on it; softening either beast into a mere metaphor of 'courage' or 'wit' collapses the figure.

divergences.locus: paragraph 7 (the closing maxim, the most misquoted line in Machiavelli)
divergences.phrase: si guarda al fine
divergences.older: one judges by the result (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: one judges by the result
divergences.note: This is the line the world has turned into 'the end justifies the means' — a sentence Machiavelli never wrote. The Italian is 'nelle azioni di tutti gli uomini, e massime de' principi, dove non è iudizio a chi reclamare, si guarda al fine.' 'Si guarda al fine' is flatly 'one looks to the end / the outcome.' Machiavelli is not laying down a moral license that good ends purify foul means; he is making a cold observation about how men actually judge — with no higher court to appeal to ('non è iudizio a chi reclamare'), a prince is assessed only by how things came out. We keep Marriott's exact 'one judges by the result,' and refuse the popular gloss, because the famous distortion inverts a description of human judgment into a principle of moral accounting Machiavelli did not assert.

divergences.phrase: parere ... religioso
divergences.older: to appear ... religious (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: to seem ... devout / religious
divergences.note: Of the five qualities a prince must counterfeit, Machiavelli singles out religion as the one it is most necessary to seem to have — 'non è cosa più necessaria a parere di avere, che questa ultima qualità.' The shock is deliberate: the appearance of piety is named the most useful of all the masks, and the chapter's veiled target (Ferdinand of Aragon, who 'preaches nothing but peace and good faith' while making war on both) is the living proof. We keep the bare verb 'seem' running through the whole passage — seem merciful, seem faithful, seem devout — never letting it slide toward 'be,' since Machiavelli's separation of seeming from being is the engine of the chapter, and religion is where he drives it home hardest.

divergences.phrase: uno de' più potenti remedii ... è non essere odiato dallo universale
divergences.older: one of the most efficacious remedies that a prince can have against conspiracies is not to be hated and despised by the people (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: One of the most effective safeguards a prince can have against conspiracies is simply not to be hated by the people at large
divergences.note: This is the chapter's structural heart, and it is easily confused with the more famous maxim 'the best fortress is not to be hated by the people' — but that line belongs to Chapter XX, not here. In Chapter XIX the Italian is 'uno de' più potenti remedii che abbia uno principe contro alle congiure, è non essere odiato dallo universale.' 'Lo universale' is the whole body of the people, the public at large, set against the handful of conspirators. The logic is cold and exact: a plotter banks on pleasing the people by killing the prince; make the people love the prince, and the plotter is left with no reward and every risk. We keep 'the people at large' for 'lo universale' to mark that it is the mass, not a faction, whose goodwill disarms the conspiracy.

divergences.phrase: vario, leggieri, effeminato, pusillanime, irresoluto
divergences.older: fickle, frivolous, effeminate, mean-spirited, irresolute (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: fickle, frivolous, soft, cowardly, or irresolute
divergences.note: Machiavelli's five vices of contempt are flung down in a flat hammering line — 'vario, leggieri, effeminato, pusillanime, irresoluto' — each the negation of a quality he demands two clauses later (greatness, courage, gravity, strength). 'Effeminato' we render 'soft' rather than the literal 'effeminate,' and 'pusillanime' as 'cowardly': the point is not effeminacy as such but the want of nerve and weight that makes a ruler beneath notice. We keep the bare asyndeton so the list lands as five blows, since the whole argument of the chapter — hated for what you do, despised for what you are — turns on holding these against the virtues of greatness and strength that answer them.

divergences.locus: paragraph 16 (Severus, the fox and the lion)
divergences.phrase: seppe bene usare la persona del golpe e del lione ... uno ferocissimo lione et una astutissima golpe
divergences.older: he knew well how to counterfeit the fox and the lion ... a most valiant lion and a most cunning fox (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: he knew how to play the part of the fox and the lion ... a most ferocious lion and a most cunning fox
divergences.note: The fox-and-lion image was set out in Chapter XVIII; here Severus is its proof — the new prince who held power by being both at once. The Italian is 'seppe bene usare la persona del golpe e del lione' — literally to use the 'persona,' the role or mask, of each. Marriott's 'counterfeit' tips it toward mere fakery; we keep 'play the part,' which holds both the performance and the genuine doubleness Machiavelli means. The closing verdict, 'lo troverrà uno ferocissimo lione et una astutissima golpe,' we render 'a most ferocious lion and a most cunning fox,' keeping the superlatives and the order; Marriott's 'valiant' softens 'ferocissimo,' which is sheer ferocity, not valor. This is the model the chapter finally holds up — Severus' prowess, not Marcus' virtue, is what a new prince must learn.

divergences.phrase: armandoli, quelle arme diventono tue ... di sudditi si fanno tua partigiani
divergences.older: by arming them, those arms become yours ... and your subjects become your adherents (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: by arming them, those arms become yours ... and your subjects become your partisans
divergences.note: The cold mechanism at the heart of the chapter, and we hold it flat to the Italian: 'armandoli, quelle arme diventono tue, diventono fedeli quelli che ti sono sospetti, e quelli che erano fedeli si mantengono, e di sudditi si fanno tua partigiani.' The logic is one of ownership, not gratitude — the weapon you put in a man's hand is now yours, because he wields it for you, so arming the doubtful converts them. We keep 'partisans' for 'partigiani' rather than the paler 'adherents,' since Machiavelli means men actively committed to your side, not mere followers. The point is counter-intuitive and must not be softened: a new prince makes himself safer by handing out arms, never by confiscating them.

divergences.phrase: la migliore fortezza che sia, è non essere odiato dal populo
divergences.older: the best possible fortress is — not to be hated by the people (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the best fortress there is, is not to be hated by the people
divergences.note: The hammer-blow the whole chapter is built to deliver, and we keep it bare and word-for-word with the tradition. The Italian is 'la migliore fortezza che sia, è non essere odiato dal populo; perché, ancora che tu abbi le fortezze, et il populo ti abbi in odio, le non ti salvono.' Machiavelli's stone-and-mortar word 'fortezza' is turned against itself: the only wall that holds is the people's goodwill, and no actual fortress will save a hated prince, because 'foreigners are never lacking to come to the aid' of a people in arms. We render 'odiato' as the blunt 'hated,' never softening it to 'disliked' or 'resented,' since the negative form is the argument — Machiavelli does not promise that being loved is a fortress, only that being hated dissolves every other one.

divergences.phrase: la contessa di Furlì ... non essere odiata dal populo che avere le fortezze
divergences.older: the Countess of Forli ... it would have been safer for her, both then and before, not to have been hated by the people than to have had the fortresses (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the Countess of Forlì ... both then and earlier it would have been safer for her not to have been hated by the people than to have had her fortresses
divergences.note: The single test case Machiavelli allows, and he turns it against fortresses even so. Caterina Sforza's castle at Forlì did save her once, after her husband Count Girolamo Riario was murdered — but only because circumstances barred any foreigner from backing the rising. When Cesare Borgia came and the people sided with him, the same fortress was worthless. We keep the proper nouns and the historical exactness intact (Girolamo killed, help awaited from Milan, then Borgia's attack), because the example is the proof: the one time a fortress worked, it worked by luck of circumstance, and the moment the people's hatred and a foreign army combined, the walls counted for nothing. The verdict 'safer not to have been hated than to have had the fortresses' must land flat, with no consolation added to the stones.

divergences.phrase: vero amico, o vero nimico
divergences.older: a true friend or a downright enemy (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: a true friend or a downright enemy
divergences.note: The cold heart of the chapter, and we hold it word for word with the tradition. The Italian is 'È ancora stimato uno principe quando elli è vero amico o vero inimico, cioè quando sanza alcuno respetto si scuopre in favore di alcuno contro a un altro.' Machiavelli's whole counsel here cuts against the prudent instinct to keep your options open: a prince earns esteem precisely by refusing to hedge — by 'discovering' himself, declaring openly and without reservation. We keep 'downright enemy' (rather than a flatter 'real enemy') because the doubled bluntness of 'vero ... vero' is the point: it is the open, unmistakable commitment, friend or foe, that wins respect, and the man who will not choose wins only contempt.

divergences.phrase: li principi mal risoluti ... il più delle volte rovinano
divergences.older: irresolute princes, to avoid present dangers, generally follow the neutral path, and are generally ruined (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: irresolute princes, to escape the dangers of the moment, usually take the neutral road, and usually come to ruin
divergences.note: Machiavelli's verdict on neutrality, and we keep its grim symmetry. The Italian is 'E li principi mal risoluti, per fuggire e' presenti periculi, seguono il più delle volte quella via neutrale, e il più delle volte rovinano.' The repeated 'il più delle volte' (most of the time) is the sting: neutrality is the coward's road, taken to dodge today's risk, and most of the time it does not save him — it destroys him. Neutrality earns the hatred of the victor (whose prey you become) and the contempt of the loser (who will not shelter you); to sit out a war between your neighbors is to be left, in the Roman legate's words, 'the prize of whoever wins.' Nothing is softened: irresolution is named for the ruin it brings.

divergences.phrase: tenendo occupati li animi di quelli baroni ... non pensando a innovare
divergences.older: he held the minds of the barons of Castile occupied in thinking of the war and not anticipating any innovations (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: he kept the minds of the barons of Castile so absorbed in the war that they never saw what was being prepared
divergences.note: The mechanism beneath Ferdinand's 'great enterprises,' and the chapter's quiet lesson in misdirection. The Italian is 'tenne occupati li animi di quelli baroni di Castiglia, li quali, pensando a quella guerra, non pensavano a innovare.' The great campaign is not only glory — it is a screen: while the barons' minds are fixed on Granada, Ferdinand is quietly building 'reputazione e imperio sopra di loro,' reputation and authority over them, without their noticing. We render 'non pensavano a innovare' as 'never saw what was being prepared' rather than the stiff 'not anticipating any innovations,' to keep the cold point that grand undertakings serve to occupy and distract a prince's own people while he tightens his grip on them.

divergences.phrase: l'uno intende da sé, l'altro discerne quello che altri intende, e il terzo non intende né sé né gli altri
divergences.older: one which comprehends by itself; another which appreciates what others comprehended; and a third which neither comprehends by itself nor by the showing of others (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: one that understands things for itself; one that grasps what another has understood; and one that understands neither for itself nor through anyone else
divergences.note: The chapter's most famous passage, and the rhythm is the argument: three minds set out in flat parallel and then graded — 'quel primo è eccellentissimo, el secondo eccellente, el terzo inutile.' The crux is the middle term, 'discerne quello che altri intende': not merely 'appreciates,' which softens it, but discerns or grasps what someone else has worked out. Machiavelli's point is precise and unflattering to Pandolfo — the second-best ruler cannot originate, but he can recognize a good idea when his minister brings it. We keep the three clauses bare and balanced and hold the single verb 'understand' across all three (intende), so the descending scale lands cleanly: understands for himself, understands what another understood, understands nothing at all.

divergences.phrase: quando tu vedi el ministro pensare più a sé che a te, e che in tutte le azioni vi ricerca dentro l'utile suo
divergences.older: when you see the servant thinking more of his own interests than of yours, and seeking inwardly his own profit in everything (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: When you see the minister thinking more of himself than of you, and seeking his own profit in everything he handles
divergences.note: Marriott renders 'ministro' as 'servant' throughout, but Machiavelli's 'ministro' is the high officer who runs the prince's affairs — the secretary or chief counselor, not a household servant. We use 'minister' to keep the rank exact, since the whole chapter is about the men closest to power. The test itself is kept blunt and unsoftened: the disqualifying sign is the man who 'pensa più a sé che a te' and hunts his own 'utile' (profit, advantage) in every action. Machiavelli draws no moral line here, only a structural one — a man who keeps any part of his attention for himself cannot be wholly the prince's, and so cannot be trusted with the prince's state.

divergences.phrase: onorandolo, faccendolo ricco, obligandoselo, partecipandogli li onori e carichi
divergences.older: honouring him, enriching him, doing him kindnesses, sharing with him the honours and cares (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: to honor him, make him rich, put him in his debt, share with him both honors and burdens
divergences.note: The prince's method for binding a good minister is a cold piece of engineering, not generosity, and we keep it so. 'Obligandoselo' is not vaguely 'doing him kindnesses' but putting him under obligation — making him owe — so the bond runs the prince's way. 'Carichi' we render 'burdens' rather than Marriott's softer 'cares': the prince shares the weight of office, not merely worries. The aim, stated plainly in what follows, is that the minister be so loaded with honors, riches, and office that he can want no more and so has nothing to gain by turning — he 'cannot stand without the prince.' The whole calculus is one of dependence deliberately manufactured, and nothing in it should read as warmth.

divergences.phrase: dipoi deliberare da sé a suo modo
divergences.older: and afterwards form his own conclusions (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: and afterwards decide for himself, in his own way
divergences.note: The hinge of the whole method. After questioning his wise men widely, the prince must 'deliberare da sé a suo modo' — deliberate by himself, in his own fashion. Marriott's 'form his own conclusions' catches the sense but loses the two stressed words: 'da sé' (alone, by himself) and 'a suo modo' (his own way, on his own terms). We keep both, because the chapter's argument turns on them — counsel is gathered from many, but the decision is the prince's alone, and the discipline of deciding alone is exactly what saves him from being pulled apart by his advisers, as Maximilian is.

divergences.phrase: come ognuno ti può dire el vero, ti manca la reverenzia
divergences.older: but when every one may tell you the truth, respect for you abates (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: But once everyone may speak the truth to you, your reverence dwindles
divergences.note: The cold paradox the chapter is built on. The only guard against flatterers is to show that truth-telling does not offend you; but if you throw that door open to everyone, 'ti manca la reverenzia' — you lose your reverence, the awe that holds men in check. Marriott's 'respect abates' is accurate but flat; we keep the stronger 'reverenzia' as 'reverence,' since Machiavelli's point is not mere esteem but the distance that makes a prince obeyed. The third course — a few licensed truth-tellers, no more — is his exit from the trap, and the trap only bites if 'reverence' carries its full weight.

divergences.phrase: li buoni consigli, da qualunque venghino, conviene naschino dalla prudenza del principe, e non la prudenza del principe da' buoni consigli
divergences.older: good counsels, whencesoever they come, are born of the wisdom of the prince, and not the wisdom of the prince from good counsels (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: good counsel, wherever it comes from, must be born of the prince's own wisdom, and not the prince's wisdom of good counsel
divergences.note: The chapter's hammer-blow, and we hold it tight to the Italian's chiasmus. Machiavelli reverses the comfortable assumption that a clever council can prop up a dull prince: the causation runs the other way. 'Conviene naschino dalla prudenza del principe' — good counsel must be BORN of the prince's own prudence; it is his judgment that makes counsel good, sifts it, and reconciles it, not the counsel that makes him wise. We keep 'prudenza' as 'wisdom' (the settled rendering here) and preserve the exact mirrored clauses, since the whole chapter exists to drive this reversal home: nothing is softened, nothing added — a prince who is not wise himself cannot be saved by good advice.

divergences.phrase: non accusino la fortuna, ma la ignavia loro
divergences.older: do not let our princes accuse fortune for the loss of their principalities ... but rather their own sloth (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: let our princes ... not blame fortune but their own sloth
divergences.note: This is the cold hinge of the chapter, and it must land bare. The Italian is 'non accusino la fortuna, ma la ignavia loro' — let them blame not fortune but their own 'ignavia,' indolence, slackness, the failure to act. Per this edition's settled rendering, fortuna stays 'fortune' (never softened to 'bad luck' as an excuse), since the whole point is that the princes reach for fortune precisely as an excuse, and Machiavelli yanks it away: the fault was never chance but their own sloth. We keep 'sloth' over 'indolence' for its blunt force and hold the antithesis flat, fortune against sloth, so the accusation cannot be dodged.

divergences.phrase: è comune difetto delli uomini, nelle bonacce, non pensare alle tempeste
divergences.older: it is a common defect in man not to make any provision in the calm against the tempest (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: it is the common failing of men not to reckon on the storm while the weather is fair
divergences.note: Machiavelli reaches for a sailor's image: 'nelle bonacce, non pensare alle tempeste' — in the dead calm ('bonaccia'), to give no thought to the storms. Marriott's 'provision in the calm against the tempest' keeps the sense but stiffens it. We render it 'reckon on the storm while the weather is fair' to keep the weather metaphor alive and the rebuke plain — the failing is not bad luck but a refusal of foresight, the same fault Machiavelli faults the Romans for not having in Chapter III. Nothing is added; the storm is already in the Italian.

divergences.phrase: quelle difese solamente sono buone, sono certe, sono durabili, che dependono da te proprio e dalla virtù tua
divergences.older: those only are reliable, certain, and durable that depend on yourself and your valour (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the only defenses that are sound, sure, and lasting are those that depend on yourself and your own prowess
divergences.note: The chapter's final verdict and the whole book in miniature. The Italian rings three flat adjectives — 'buone ... certe ... durabili' — and turns on 'da te proprio e dalla virtù tua': on yourself and your own virtù. Per this edition's settled rendering, virtù is 'prowess' here, not Marriott's 'valour' (too narrowly martial) and never moral 'virtue,' since the argument is that only the force and skill you command yourself can be relied on. We hold the triad bare and end on 'your own prowess,' so the cold rule lands: borrowed defenses fail, only your own hold.

sections.label: Chapter I
sections.title: How Many Kinds of Principalities There Are, and By What Means They Are Acquired

segments.text: Every state, every power that has ever held sway over men, has been and is either a republic or a principality. Principalities are either hereditary, where the ruling family has held power for generations, or they are new.

New principalities are either wholly new, as Milan was to Francesco Sforza, or they are limbs grafted onto the hereditary state of the prince who acquires them, as the kingdom of Naples was to the King of Spain. Dominions taken this way are either used to living under a prince or used to being free; and they are won either by the prince's own arms or by the arms of others, by luck or by skill.

sections.label: Chapter II
sections.title: Concerning Hereditary Principalities

segments.text: I will set aside any discussion of republics, since I have written about them at length elsewhere, and address myself to principalities alone. Keeping to the order I laid out above, I will examine how such principalities are to be governed and held.

I say at once that hereditary states, long accustomed to the line of their prince, are far less troublesome to hold than new ones. It is enough for the prince not to break with the customs of his ancestors, and to bend with circumstances as they arise; a man of merely ordinary ability can keep his footing, unless some extraordinary and overwhelming force strips him of it. And even if he is stripped of it, the moment any setback befalls the one who seized his place, he wins it back.

Take, for example, the Duke of Ferrara here in Italy. He could not have withstood the assault of the Venetians in '84, nor that of Pope Julius in 1510, had he not been long settled in his domains. For the hereditary prince has less reason and less need to give offense, and so he is the more loved; and unless monstrous vices make him hated, it stands to reason that his subjects will be naturally well disposed toward him. In the long age and continuity of his rule, the memories and motives that drive men to change are extinguished — for one upheaval always leaves behind the toothing on which the next is built.

sections.label: Chapter III
sections.title: Concerning Mixed Principalities

segments.text: The real difficulties begin with a new principality. Take first the case of one that is not entirely new but joined onto a state the ruler already holds, so that the two together make up what we might call a mixed principality. Here the trouble comes from a flaw built into every new acquisition: men are willing to change rulers because they believe the change will improve their lot, and that belief moves them to take up arms against the man in power. They are wrong, of course. Experience soon teaches them they have only made things worse. And that follows from another natural and ordinary necessity: a new prince is always forced to burden the people he has just taken over with his troops, and with countless other hardships that conquest brings in its train.

So you find that you have made enemies of everyone you injured in seizing the principality, while you cannot keep the friendship of those who put you in power, since you are unable to satisfy them as fully as they expected — and you cannot move hard against them either, because you are in their debt. For however strong your army, you always need the goodwill of the local people to take and hold a province.

These are the reasons why Louis XII, King of France, took Milan in an instant and lost it just as fast. The first time, Lodovico's own forces were enough to throw him out: the very people who had opened the gates, finding the future they had hoped for had not come, would not stomach the abuses of their new ruler. It is quite true that when a prince retakes a rebellious province a second time, he does not lose it so easily, because he uses the rebellion as a pretext to punish the guilty, expose the suspect, and shore up his weak points without much restraint. The first time, all it took to make France lose Milan was Duke Lodovico rattling the borders; the second time, it took the whole world combining against the king, his armies broken and chased out of Italy — and that followed from the causes already named.

Even so, Milan was wrested from France both times. The general reasons for the first loss have been given; it remains to set out the reasons for the second, and to ask what resources the king had — what anyone in his position would have had — to hold his conquest more securely than he did.

Now, the territories a ruler annexes to his existing state are either of the same country and language as his own, or they are not. When they are, holding them is easy, especially if they are not used to governing themselves. To make your grip secure it is enough to wipe out the line of the prince who ruled them, because, with everything else in their old life left untouched and their customs much like yours, the two peoples will settle down together quietly — as we have seen in Brittany, Burgundy, Gascony, and Normandy, bound to France for so long. There may be some difference of language, but the customs are alike, and the peoples get along easily. Whoever annexes such lands and means to keep them has only two things to watch: that the family of the former lord is extinguished, and that he changes neither their laws nor their taxes. Then in a very short time the new territory fuses into one body with the old.

But when you acquire states in a region that differs in language, customs, and laws, the difficulties are real, and it takes good luck and great skill to hold them. One of the best remedies, and one of the most solid, is for the man who has taken them to go and live there himself. That makes his hold steadier and more lasting — as it has for the Turk in Greece, who, for all the other measures he took to keep that country, could never have held it had he not settled there. Living on the spot, you see disorders the moment they sprout and can deal with them at once; living far off, you hear of them only once they are large, and by then there is no cure. On top of that, your officials cannot strip the country bare; the people are content, because the prince is close at hand to appeal to; so those inclined to be loyal have more reason to love him, and those inclined otherwise more reason to fear him. Anyone planning to attack such a state from outside will think twice: as long as the prince lives there, it can only be torn from him with the greatest difficulty.

The next best course is to plant colonies in one or two places that serve as keys to the country. You must do this, or else keep a large force of cavalry and infantry stationed there. Colonies cost a prince little or nothing: he sends them out and maintains them cheaply, and the only people he injures are the few whose fields and houses he takes to give the newcomers — a small minority. Those he injures, left poor and scattered, can never harm him, while everyone else, untouched, stays quiet, and is careful besides not to step out of line, for fear of being dispossessed like the others. In short, colonies are cheap, more loyal, and do less harm; and the few who are harmed, being poor and scattered, can do nothing about it. On which note, men ought either to be caressed or crushed, for they will avenge small injuries but cannot avenge grave ones; so the harm you do a man should be such that you need never fear his revenge.

Holding the country with soldiers instead of colonies costs far more, since the whole revenue of the state is eaten up keeping the garrison, so that the gain turns into a loss; and it gives far more offense, since billeting the troops up and down inflicts hardship on the whole population, until everyone is your enemy — enemies who, beaten in their own homes, can still do you harm. By every measure, then, a garrison is as useless as a colony is useful.

Again, a prince who takes over a country unlike his own in these respects should make himself the head and protector of his weaker neighbors, work to weaken the stronger ones, and above all see to it that no foreigner as powerful as himself ever gets a foothold there by any mishap. For such a foreigner will always be let in by the discontented within, whether out of excessive ambition or out of fear — as we have already seen. It was the Aetolians who brought the Romans into Greece; and in every other country the Romans entered, it was the inhabitants who brought them. The way of things is that the moment a powerful outsider sets foot in a land, all the lesser states there rally to him, driven by their hatred of the power that ruled them. So with these lesser states he need take no trouble at all to win them over — they flock of their own accord to the position he has taken.
