He has only to see that they do not gain too much strength and authority; and then, with his own forces and their goodwill, he can easily hold down the stronger powers and remain complete master of the country. The ruler who mismanages this will quickly lose what he has won, and for as long as he keeps it will be plagued by endless troubles.

In the countries they annexed, the Romans observed these rules to the letter: they sent colonies, kept the minor powers friendly without letting them grow, held down the great ones, and would not let any strong foreign power gain authority. Greece alone is example enough. The Romans kept the Achaeans and Aetolians as friends; they humbled the kingdom of Macedon; they drove out Antiochus. Yet for all the services of the Achaeans and Aetolians, the Romans never let them enlarge their power; no persuasion of Philip's ever won them his friendship without first humbling him; and all the weight of Antiochus could not make them grant him so much as a single holding in the country. For in these cases the Romans did what every wise prince must do: look not only to present troubles but to future ones, and guard against those with all their energy. Trouble foreseen is easily cured; let it come close before you act, and the medicine arrives too late, for the disease has grown incurable. It is here as the doctors say of consumption: early on it is easy to cure and hard to detect, but with time, left undetected and untreated, it becomes easy to detect and hard to cure. So it is in affairs of state. Foresee the evils brewing — which only a wise man can do — and they are quickly set right; let them go unseen until they have grown so plain that everyone sees them, and there is no longer any remedy. The Romans, then, saw their troubles coming and dealt with them at once. They would not let a danger run on merely to dodge a war, because they knew that war is never avoided, only postponed to another man's advantage. So they chose to fight Philip and Antiochus in Greece, rather than have to fight them later in Italy. They could have ducked both wars at the time, but they chose not to. They never trusted that maxim forever on the lips of the wise men of our own day — "enjoy the benefits of time" — but trusted instead the benefits of their own skill and foresight. For time sweeps everything before it, and can bring good as easily as ill, and ill as easily as good.

But let us turn back to France and ask whether she did any of these things. I will speak of Louis, not Charles, since Louis held ground in Italy longer and his conduct is the clearer to read; and you will see he did the very opposite of what must be done to hold a state of differing parts.

King Louis was brought into Italy by the ambition of the Venetians, who meant to seize half of Lombardy through his coming. I do not blame the king for the move: wanting a foothold in Italy and having no friends there — every door shut to him, in fact, by Charles's earlier conduct — he was forced to take whatever friendships he could get, and his design would have succeeded fast had he not blundered elsewhere. Having taken Lombardy, the king at once recovered the standing Charles had thrown away: Genoa gave in; the Florentines became his friends; the Marquess of Mantua, the Duke of Ferrara, the Bentivogli, the Lady of Forli, the Lords of Faenza, Pesaro, Rimini, Camerino, and Piombino, the Lucchese, the Pisans, the Sienese — all came forward to be his friend. Only then could the Venetians grasp the recklessness of their gamble: to gain two towns in Lombardy, they had made the king master of two-thirds of Italy.

Consider how little trouble it would have cost the king to hold his position in Italy, had he kept to the rules laid out above and kept all those friends safe and protected. They were many, but weak and timid — some afraid of the Church, some of the Venetians — and so they would always have been bound to stand with him, and through them he could easily have secured himself against the powers that remained strong. But no sooner was he in Milan than he did the opposite: he helped Pope Alexander seize the Romagna. It never crossed his mind that by this he was weakening himself, throwing away his friends and the very men who had thrown themselves into his lap, while he built up the Church, adding great temporal power to its spiritual authority and so making it stronger still. Having made this first error, he was dragged into others: to check Alexander's ambition and keep him from making himself master of Tuscany, Louis was forced to come into Italy himself.

And as if it were not enough to have built up the Church and stripped himself of friends, Louis — coveting the kingdom of Naples — split it with the King of Spain. So where he had been the chief arbiter of Italy, he brought in a partner, giving the ambitious and the malcontents of that country a refuge to run to; and where he could have left a king of his own there, beholden to him, he drove that man out and installed one strong enough to drive out Louis himself.

The desire to acquire is a thoroughly natural and ordinary thing, and when men can do it, they will, and be praised for it rather than blamed. But when they cannot, and try anyway by any means, that is the folly that earns blame. If France could have struck at Naples with her own forces, she should have; if she could not, she should never have divided it. And if the partition of Lombardy with the Venetians could be excused on the ground that it bought her a foothold in Italy, this partition of Naples deserves blame, for it had no such necessity to excuse it.

So Louis made these five mistakes: he destroyed the lesser powers; he built up the strength of one of the greater powers in Italy; he brought in a powerful foreigner; he did not settle in the country; and he planted no colonies. These errors, while he lived, might still not have ruined him, had he not made a sixth — stripping the Venetians of their lands. For had he not aggrandized the Church or brought Spain into Italy, it would have been entirely reasonable, even necessary, to humble Venice; but once he had taken those other steps, he should never have agreed to her ruin. As long as the Venetians were strong, they would always have kept others off any designs on Lombardy — partly because Venice would never have allowed it unless she could be mistress there herself, and partly because no one else would want to take Lombardy from France only to hand it to Venice, and would lack the nerve to defy them both.

And should someone object, "King Louis ceded the Romagna to Alexander and Naples to Spain to avoid a war," I answer, for the reasons already given, that you should never let a disorder run on to avoid a war, because the war is not avoided — only deferred to your disadvantage. And should someone else plead the promise the king had given the Pope, to back his enterprise in exchange for the annulment of his marriage and the cardinal's cap for Rouen, I refer him to what I shall say later about the faith of princes and how it ought to be kept.

So King Louis lost Lombardy for failing to observe a single one of the rules kept by those who have taken countries and meant to hold them. There is no miracle in this — it is reasonable and entirely natural. I spoke of these very matters at Nantes with the Cardinal of Rouen, at the time Valentino — as Cesare Borgia, Pope Alexander's son, was commonly called — was occupying the Romagna. When the Cardinal of Rouen remarked to me that the Italians did not understand war, I replied that the French did not understand statecraft, for had they understood it they would never have let the Church grow so great. And indeed it has proven true: France was the cause of the greatness of both the Church and Spain in Italy, and those two were the cause of France's ruin. From this we draw a rule that rarely if ever fails: whoever makes another powerful ruins himself, because he builds that power up by cunning or by force, and both of these are suspect to the very man he has raised.

sections.label: Chapter IV
sections.title: Why the Kingdom of Darius, Conquered by Alexander, Did Not Rebel Against Alexander's Successors at His Death

segments.text: Given how much trouble men have in holding a newly won state, one might wonder at this: Alexander the Great made himself master of Asia in a few years, and died before it was scarcely settled. It would seem natural for the whole empire to have risen in revolt. Yet his successors held on, and met no difficulty in keeping it beyond what their own ambitions stirred up among themselves.

My answer is that all the principalities we have any record of are governed in one of two ways. Either by a prince and a body of servants who, by his favor and leave, help him govern the kingdom as his ministers; or by a prince and barons, who hold their rank not by the prince's grace but by antiquity of blood. Barons of this kind have states and subjects of their own, who acknowledge them as lords and bear them a natural affection. In the states ruled by a prince and his servants, the prince holds far greater authority, for in all his country there is no one recognized as a superior above him; and if the people obey anyone else, they do it as toward a minister and official, and feel no particular loyalty to him.

The clearest examples of these two kinds of government in our own day are the Turk and the King of France. The whole monarchy of the Turk is governed by one lord, and all the rest are his servants. He divides his kingdom into districts and sends out different administrators to govern them, shifting and replacing them as he pleases. The King of France, by contrast, stands in the midst of a great body of ancient lords, each acknowledged by subjects of his own and beloved by them. These lords have their hereditary prerogatives, which the king cannot strip away without danger to himself. So whoever weighs these two states will see that the Turk's is hard to seize but, once taken, easy to hold; while the opposite is true of France. The difficulty of seizing the Turk's state lies in this: an invader cannot be invited in by princes of the kingdom, nor hope that those around the lord will revolt and help his cause. The reasons are the ones already given. Since they are all slaves and bondmen, they are corrupted only with great difficulty, and even once corrupted they are of little use, for they cannot carry the people with them. So anyone who attacks the Turk must reckon on finding him united, and must rely on his own strength rather than on disorder among the enemy. But once the Turk is beaten and routed in the field so thoroughly that he cannot raise his armies again, there is nothing left to fear but the prince's own family; and once that line is wiped out, no one remains to be feared, since the others have no standing with the people. Just as the conqueror could expect nothing from them before his victory, so he has nothing to fear from them after it.

The reverse holds in kingdoms governed like that of France. There you can easily get in by winning over some baron of the realm, for there are always malcontents and men hungry for change. For the reasons given, such men can open the way into the state and make the victory easy. But holding it afterward brings endless difficulties, from those who helped you and from those you crushed alike. It is not enough to have wiped out the prince's line, because the lords who remain put themselves at the head of fresh risings; and since you can neither satisfy them nor destroy them, you lose that state the moment the chance presents itself.

Now, if you consider what kind of government Darius had, you will find it resembled the Turk's. So Alexander had first to beat him outright in the field and drive him from the country. After that victory, with Darius dead, the state was secure to Alexander for the reasons set out above. Had his successors held together, they could have enjoyed it in ease, for the only upheavals raised in that kingdom were the ones they stirred up themselves.

But states built like France cannot be held with any such calm. This is why the Romans faced those repeated revolts in Spain, France, and Greece — because of the many principalities in those lands. So long as the memory of them lasted, Rome's hold was never secure; but once the power and long endurance of the empire had blotted that memory out, the Romans became settled masters. And when they later fell to fighting among themselves, each could draw to his side the part of the country where his authority ran; and with the line of the former lords extinguished, those peoples acknowledged no masters but the Romans.

Weigh all this, and no one will marvel at the ease with which Alexander held the empire of Asia, or at the difficulties others have had in keeping what they took — Pyrrhus and many more. This turns not on the conqueror's having more skill or less, but on the difference in the states he takes.

sections.label: Chapter V
sections.title: How to Govern Cities or Principalities That Lived Under Their Own Laws Before They Were Annexed

segments.text: When the states you acquire have been used to living under their own laws and in freedom, there are three ways to hold them. The first is to ruin them. The second is to go and live there yourself. The third is to let them keep their own laws, exact a tribute, and set up inside the state an oligarchy that will keep it friendly to you. Such a government, knowing it owes its existence to the prince, knows too that it cannot stand without his backing and his power, and so it will do everything to uphold him. A city used to its freedom is held more easily through its own citizens, when you mean to keep it, than by any other means.

Take the Spartans and the Romans. The Spartans held Athens and Thebes by planting an oligarchy in each — and lost them both anyway. The Romans, to hold Capua, Carthage, and Numantia, dismantled them, and did not lose them. They tried to hold Greece much as the Spartans had held their cities, leaving it free under its own laws, and failed; so in the end, to keep it, they were forced to raze many of its cities. For the truth is there is no sure way to hold such places except to lay them in ruins. Whoever becomes master of a city used to living free, and does not destroy it, may expect to be destroyed by it. For in rebellion it always has a refuge in the name of liberty and its ancient privileges, which neither the passing of time nor any favor will ever make it forget. Whatever you do, whatever provision you make, unless its people are scattered and broken apart they never forget that name or those privileges, but reach for them the moment a chance appears — as Pisa did after the hundred years she had been held in bondage by the Florentines.

But when cities or provinces have been used to living under a prince, and his line is wiped out, then — schooled on the one hand to obey, and left on the other without their old master — they cannot agree on raising one of their own to the throne, and they do not know how to govern themselves. So they are slow to take up arms, and a prince can win them over and make himself secure far more easily. In republics, though, there is more life, more hatred, more hunger for revenge; the memory of their former liberty gives them no rest and never will. The safest course with them is to wipe them out, or to go and live there.

sections.label: Chapter VI
sections.title: Concerning New Principalities Acquired by One's Own Arms and Skill

segments.text: Let no one be surprised if, in speaking of principalities that are wholly new — both the prince and the state new — I reach for the very greatest examples. Men nearly always walk in paths beaten by others, shaping their own conduct by imitation; and though they can never keep entirely to another man's road, or match the skill of the men they imitate, a prudent man will still always set his feet in the paths trodden by the great and model himself on those who have been supreme, so that even if his own ability does not reach theirs, it may at least catch something of their scent. He should do as the skilled archers do: judging the mark too far off, and knowing just how far the strength of their bow will carry, they aim well above it — not to drive the arrow that high, but so that, aiming high, they may strike the mark they actually mean to hit.

I say, then, that in principalities entirely new, where there is a new prince, the difficulty of holding them is greater or less in proportion to the skill of the man who has acquired them. And since rising from private citizen to prince presupposes either skill or luck, it is plain that one or the other of these will smooth away many of the difficulties. Even so, the man who has leaned least on luck has held on the longest. It also helps that the prince, having no other state, is forced to come and live there in person.

But to come to those who became princes by their own skill and not by luck, I say that the most outstanding are Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus, and men like them. And though Moses ought not perhaps to be discussed, since he was merely carrying out what God commanded, still he deserves our admiration if only for the grace that made him worthy to speak with God. But take Cyrus and the others who won or founded kingdoms: you will find them all admirable; and if you weigh their particular deeds and methods, they will not look inferior to those of Moses, for all that he had so great a teacher. Examining their actions and their lives, you see that they owed nothing to luck except the opportunity, which handed them the raw material they could then mold into whatever shape they pleased. Without that opportunity their force of mind would have been wasted; without that force the opportunity would have come in vain.

It was necessary, then, that Moses should find the people of Israel in Egypt, enslaved and oppressed by the Egyptians, so that they would be willing to follow him to escape their bondage. It was necessary that Romulus should have no place in Alba, and be cast out at birth, if he was to become King of Rome and founder of his country. It was necessary that Cyrus should find the Persians chafing under the rule of the Medes, and the Medes gone soft and slack from a long peace. Theseus could never have shown his skill had he not found the Athenians scattered. These opportunities, then, made these men's fortune, and their own high skill let them seize the opportunity; by which their countries were ennobled and made famous.

Those who come to power by such paths of skill acquire their principality with difficulty but hold it with ease. The difficulties they meet in acquiring it spring in part from the new orders and methods they are forced to bring in to found their rule and make it secure. And it must be borne in mind that there is nothing harder to undertake, nothing more perilous to manage, nor more uncertain of success, than to set oneself up as the leader in introducing a new order of things. For the innovator makes enemies of all who did well under the old order, and finds only lukewarm defenders in those who might do well under the new. This lukewarmness comes partly from fear of their adversaries, who have the law on their side, and partly from the skepticism of men, who do not truly believe in anything new until they have had solid experience of it. So it happens that whenever those hostile to the change get the chance to attack, they do so with the fury of partisans, while the others defend so half-heartedly that the prince is endangered along with them.

It is necessary, therefore, if we mean to examine this matter properly, to ask whether these innovators stand on their own feet or depend on others — that is, whether to carry their work through they must beg, or whether they can compel. In the first case they always come to grief and accomplish nothing; but when they depend on themselves and can use force, then they are rarely in danger. This is why all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. For besides what I have already said, the temper of the people is fickle: it is easy to convince them of a thing, but hard to hold them to that conviction. So matters must be so arranged that when they no longer believe, they can be made to believe by force.

Had Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus been unarmed, they could not have made their constitutions hold for long — as happened in our own day to Fra Girolamo Savonarola, who was ruined along with his new order the moment the crowd stopped believing in him, since he had no way to keep the believers steadfast or to force the doubters to believe. Men like these, then, have great trouble carrying their work through, for all their dangers lie in the climb; but with skill they overcome them, and once they are past, and those who envied their success have been wiped out, they begin to be respected, and go on powerful, secure, honored, and content.

To these great examples I will add a lesser one, though it bears some likeness to them and can stand for all of its kind: Hiero of Syracuse. This man rose from private citizen to Prince of Syracuse, and he too owed nothing to luck but the opportunity; for the Syracusans, hard pressed, chose him as their captain, and afterward judged him worthy to be made their prince. Even as a private man his skill was so great that one who wrote of him said he lacked nothing to be a king but a kingdom. He did away with the old army and organized a new one; he dropped his old alliances and made new ones; and once he had soldiers and allies of his own, on such a foundation he could raise whatever building he liked — so that he had endured much trouble in the winning and had little in the keeping.

sections.label: Chapter VII
sections.title: Concerning New Principalities Acquired by the Arms of Others or by Fortune

segments.text: Men who rise from private citizen to prince by sheer luck have little trouble getting there, but a great deal staying there. They meet no obstacles on the way up, because they fly; the trouble comes the moment they land. Such are the men handed a state for money, or by the favor of whoever bestows it — as happened to many in Greece, in the cities of Ionia and the Hellespont, where Darius made men princes so that they would hold those cities for his security and his glory; and as happened, too, with those emperors who climbed from private station to the empire by bribing the soldiers. Men like these rest on nothing but the goodwill and the fortune of whoever raised them — two things as inconstant and unstable as any in the world. They lack both the knowledge and the means to hold their place: the knowledge, because unless a man is of great ability and force of character, it is unreasonable to expect that one who has always lived as a private citizen should suddenly know how to command; and the means, because they have no forces of their own that they can keep loyal and devoted.

States that spring up overnight, then, are like everything else in nature that is born and grows in haste: they cannot put down the roots and form the connections they need, and the first spell of bad weather destroys them. Unless, as I said, the men who become princes so suddenly are of such ability that they know at once how to hold what fortune has dropped in their laps — laying afterward the foundations that other princes lay before they rise.

On these two ways of becoming a prince — by skill or by luck — I want to set down two examples from our own time: Francesco Sforza and Cesare Borgia. Francesco, by the right means and with great skill, rose from private citizen to Duke of Milan, and what he won with a thousand hardships he kept with little trouble. Cesare Borgia, on the other hand — Duke Valentino, as the people called him — won his state through the fortunes of his father, and lost it when those fortunes failed, even though he had taken every measure and done everything a shrewd and able man should do to sink his roots into the states that the arms and fortune of others had handed him.

For, as I said above, the man who has not laid his foundations first may with great skill lay them afterward, but only at much trouble to the builder and much risk to the building. Look at every step the duke took, and you will see he laid solid foundations for his future power. I think it worth setting them out, for I know no better lesson to give a new prince than the example of his actions. And if in the end his measures failed him, that was no fault of his, but the extraordinary and extreme malignity of fortune.

When Pope Alexander VI set out to make his son the duke a great man, he faced no end of difficulties, both immediate and to come. First, he saw no way to make him master of any state that was not the Church's; and he knew that if he tried to carve one out of Church lands, the Duke of Milan and the Venetians would never stand for it, since Faenza and Rimini were already under Venetian protection. On top of that, he saw that the arms of Italy — especially the ones he might have leaned on — were in the hands of men who had every reason to dread the growth of papal power: namely the Orsini, the Colonna, and their following. He had to upset this whole arrangement, then, and throw the Italian powers into confusion, so as to make himself safe master of part of their lands. This proved easy, for he found the Venetians, moved by reasons of their own, bent on bringing the French back into Italy. Not only did he not oppose this — he made it easier still by dissolving King Louis's former marriage. So the king came into Italy with Venetian help and Alexander's blessing, and was no sooner in Milan than the Pope had troops from him for the campaign on the Romagna, which surrendered to the duke on the king's reputation alone. So the duke took the Romagna and beat the Colonna. But when he wanted to hold what he had and push further, two things stood in his way. One was that his own forces did not look loyal; the other was the goodwill of France. He feared, that is, that the Orsini troops he was using would fail him — that they might not only block him from winning more, but even seize what he had already won — and that the king might do the same. He had his warning about the Orsini when, after the capture of Faenza, he attacked Bologna and saw how grudgingly they went into that assault. And he learned the king's mind when, after taking the duchy of Urbino, he moved on Tuscany and the king made him pull back. After that, the duke resolved to depend no longer on the arms and the luck of others.

His first step was to weaken the Orsini and Colonna parties in Rome. He won over all their gentleman adherents, taking them into his own household, putting them on good pay, and honoring them — each according to his rank — with offices and commands, so that within a few months their old loyalty to the factions melted away and fastened entirely on the duke. Then he waited for a chance to crush the Orsini, the Colonna following having already been scattered. The chance came soon, and he used it well. For the Orsini, realizing at last that the rise of the duke and the Church meant their own ruin, called a council at Magione, in the country near Perugia. Out of that came the revolt at Urbino and the uprisings in the Romagna, and no end of danger to the duke — all of which he overcame with French help. With his authority restored, and unwilling to leave it at the mercy of the French or any other outside force, he turned to cunning. He concealed his intentions so well that, through the mediation of Signor Paolo — whom he was careful to secure with every attention, lavishing money, fine clothes, and horses on him — the Orsini were reconciled to him; and their own gullibility delivered them into his hands at Senigallia. Having wiped out the leaders and turned their followers into his friends, the duke had laid more than adequate foundations for his power, holding all the Romagna along with the duchy of Urbino — and with the people now beginning to taste the good of his rule, he won them over entirely. This last point deserves notice and is worth imitating, so I will not pass it by.

When the duke took the Romagna, he found it had been governed by feeble masters who plundered their subjects rather than ruled them, and gave them more cause for discord than for unity, so that the whole province was rife with robbery, feuds, and every kind of violence. He judged that to restore it to peace and obedience he would have to give it a good governor. So he set over it Messer Remirro de Orco, a swift and brutal man, and gave him absolute power. In short order this man brought the country to peace and unity, and won great renown by it. Then the duke decided that such unchecked authority was no longer wise, fearing it would breed hatred; so he set up a civil court in the heart of the province, under a most able president, where every city had its own advocate. And because he knew that the late severities had earned him some hatred, he wanted — to purge men's minds and win the people over completely — to show that whatever cruelty had been done sprang not from him but from the harsh nature of his minister. Seizing on this pretext, one morning he had Remirro laid out in the piazza at Cesena in two pieces, with a block of wood and a bloody knife beside him. The ferocity of that spectacle left the people at once satisfied and stupefied.

But let me return to where I began. With the duke now strong enough, and largely secured against immediate dangers — having armed himself in his own way and broken most of the neighboring forces that could have harmed him — what remained, if he meant to keep pressing his conquest, was France. He knew the king, awake too late to his blunder, would no longer back him. So from this point he began to look for new alliances, and to hold France at arm's length over the campaign she was then waging toward the kingdom of Naples against the Spaniards besieging Gaeta. His aim was to secure himself against the French; and he would have managed it quickly, had Alexander lived.

So much for how he handled the present. As for the future, his first fear was that a new head of the Church might not be his friend, and might try to take back what Alexander had given him. Against this he resolved to guard four ways. First, by exterminating the families of all the lords he had stripped of their lands, so as to deny the Pope that pretext. Second, by winning over all the gentlemen of Rome, so as to hold the Pope in check through them, as already noted. Third, by bringing the College of Cardinals as far as he could onto his side. Fourth, by gaining so much power before the Pope's death that he could withstand the first shock on his own. By the time Alexander died, he had achieved three of these four. He had killed as many of the dispossessed lords as he could lay hands on, and few had slipped away; he had won over the Roman gentlemen; and he had the largest party in the College. As for fresh conquests, he meant to make himself master of Tuscany; he already held Perugia and Piombino, and had taken Pisa under his protection. And since he no longer had to mind France — the French having by now been driven out of the kingdom of Naples by the Spaniards, so that both sides had to court his goodwill — he pounced on Pisa. After that, Lucca and Siena gave in at once, partly out of hatred of the Florentines and partly out of fear of them; and the Florentines would have had no defense left. Had he gone on prospering as he was prospering the year Alexander died, he would have built up such power and standing that he could have stood on his own feet, no longer leaning on the luck and the forces of others but solely on his own power and skill.

But Alexander died five years after the duke first drew his sword. He left him with only the state of the Romagna firmly consolidated and everything else up in the air, caught between two of the most powerful hostile armies, and himself sick to death. Yet there was in the duke such boldness and such ability, and he understood so well how men are to be won or lost, and so firm were the foundations he had laid in so short a time, that had he not had those armies at his back, or had he simply been in good health, he would have come through every difficulty. And the proof that his foundations were sound is that the Romagna held for him more than a month. In Rome, though barely half alive, he stayed secure; and though the Baglioni, the Vitelli, and the Orsini came to Rome, they could do nothing against him. If he could not make whomever he wished pope, at least he could keep out anyone he did not want. Had he only been in sound health when Alexander died, everything would have gone easily for him. He told me himself, the day Julius II was elected, that he had foreseen everything that might happen at his father's death and had a remedy ready for all of it — except that he had never imagined that, when the death came, he too would be at the point of death.

Weighing up all the duke's actions, I cannot find it in me to fault him. On the contrary, I think — as I have said — that he should be held up as a model for everyone who comes to power by the fortune or the arms of others. For with his great spirit and his far-reaching aims, he could not have conducted himself otherwise, and it was only the shortness of Alexander's life and his own sickness that wrecked his designs. So a man who finds it necessary, in a new principality, to make himself safe against his enemies, to win friends, to conquer by force or by fraud, to make himself loved and feared by the people, to be followed and revered by his soldiers, to wipe out those who have the power or the reason to harm him, to replace the old order with a new one, to be at once severe and gracious, generous and openhanded, to disband a disloyal army and raise his own, to keep on such terms with kings and princes that they must either help him gladly or strike at him with caution — such a man can find no fresher example than the actions of this one.

The one thing he can be blamed for is the election of Julius II, where his choice was a bad one. As I said, though he could not make a pope to his own liking, he had it in his power to block anyone he did not want; and he should never have let any cardinal reach the papacy who had been injured by him, or who, once pope, would have reason to fear him — for men strike out of fear as readily as out of hatred. Among those he had injured were San Pietro in Vincoli, Colonna, San Giorgio, and Ascanio. All the rest, on becoming pope, would have had cause to fear him, except Rouen and the Spaniards — the Spaniards by ties of blood and obligation, Rouen by his strength, being backed by the kingdom of France. So above all the duke should have made a Spaniard pope; failing that, he should have agreed to Rouen and never to San Pietro in Vincoli. Whoever thinks that new favors make great men forget old injuries deceives himself. The duke, then, erred in this election, and it was the cause of his final ruin.

sections.label: Chapter VIII
sections.title: Concerning Those Who Have Obtained a Principality by Wickedness

segments.text: A private citizen can rise to be prince in two more ways, neither of which can be put down wholly to luck or to skill, and I do not mean to pass them over in silence — though one of them might be treated more fully where I discuss republics. These are: coming to power by some wicked and criminal path, or being raised to the rule of one's country by the favor of one's fellow-citizens. I will illustrate the first by two examples, one ancient and one modern, without going further into its merits; for I judge these two enough for anyone forced to follow such methods.

Agathocles the Sicilian became King of Syracuse not just from private life but from a low and abject station. The son of a potter, he led a disgraceful life at every turn of his fortunes. Yet he matched his disgraces with such force of mind and body that, taking up soldiering, he climbed through the ranks to become Praetor of Syracuse. Set in that office, he resolved to make himself prince — to hold by violence, and beholden to no one, what had been granted him by consent. He came to an understanding on this with Hamilcar the Carthaginian, who was then campaigning with his army in Sicily. One morning he assembled the people and senate of Syracuse, as though he had matters of state to lay before them, and at a prearranged signal his soldiers killed every senator and the richest of the citizens. With them dead, he seized and held the rule of the city, and no one stirred against him. And though the Carthaginians twice routed him and at last laid siege to him, he not only defended his city but, leaving part of his men to hold it, crossed with the rest into Africa, and in short order lifted the siege of Syracuse. The Carthaginians, driven to extremity, were forced to come to terms with him: they left Sicily to him and contented themselves with Africa.

Anyone who weighs the actions and the gifts of this man will see little or nothing he owed to fortune, since he came to the top, as I have said, not by anyone's favor but step by step through the army, winning each step through a thousand hardships and dangers, and then holding power by many bold and hazardous strokes. Yet it cannot be called skill to slaughter your fellow-citizens, to betray your friends, to be without faith, without mercy, without religion. Such methods may win you power, but not glory. For if you weigh his courage in walking into danger and out again, and his greatness of spirit in bearing and beating down hardship, there is no reason to rank him below the finest captain who ever lived. All the same, his savage cruelty and inhumanity, and his measureless crimes, forbid us to count him among the greatest men. What he achieved, then, cannot be put down to either fortune or skill.

In our own time, under Pope Alexander the Sixth, there was Oliverotto da Fermo. Orphaned years before, he was raised by his maternal uncle, Giovanni Fogliani, and sent young to soldier under Paolo Vitelli, so that, trained in that discipline, he might rise to high rank in the profession. When Paolo died, he served under his brother Vitellozzo, and being quick-witted and vigorous in body and mind, he soon became the foremost man in that service. But finding it a poor thing to serve under others, he resolved to seize Fermo — with the help of certain men of Fermo who held the slavery of their city dearer than its freedom, and with the backing of the Vitelli. So he wrote to Giovanni Fogliani that, having been away from home for many years, he wished to come and see him and his city and to take some look at his own inheritance; and since he had labored for nothing but honor, he wanted his fellow-citizens to see he had not wasted his time, and so meant to come in style, escorted by a hundred horsemen, his friends and retainers. He begged Giovanni to see to it that the people of Fermo received him with honor — which would reflect not only on himself but on Giovanni, who had brought him up.

Giovanni did not stint any courtesy owed his nephew. He had him honorably received by the Fermians and lodged him in his own house. There, after a few days spent making the arrangements his wicked design required, Oliverotto gave a grand banquet and invited Giovanni Fogliani and the leading men of Fermo. When the food and all the other entertainments customary at such banquets were done, Oliverotto cunningly turned to weighty matters, speaking of the greatness of Pope Alexander and his son Cesare and their undertakings. Giovanni and the others took up the talk, but Oliverotto suddenly rose, saying such things ought to be discussed somewhere more private, and withdrew to an inner room, with Giovanni and the rest of the citizens following him in. No sooner were they seated than soldiers burst from hidden places and butchered Giovanni and all the rest. After the killings Oliverotto mounted his horse and rode through the town, and laid siege to the chief magistrate in the palace, until the people, in fear, were forced to obey him and to set up a government with himself as prince. He put to death everyone who, being discontented, might have harmed him, and shored up his position with new ordinances, civil and military, so that within the single year he held the principality he was not only secure in Fermo but a terror to all his neighbors. He would have been as hard to dislodge as Agathocles, had he not let himself be outwitted by Cesare Borgia, who took him along with the Orsini and the Vitelli at Sinigaglia, as I have already told. There, one year after he committed his parricide, he was strangled, together with Vitellozzo, the man who had been his master in prowess and in crime.

Some may wonder how it can be that Agathocles, and others like him, after endless treachery and cruelty, can live long and secure in their own country, defend themselves against outside enemies, and never be conspired against by their own citizens — while many others, for all their cruelty, have failed to hold their state even in settled times, let alone in the doubtful times of war. I believe this turns on whether cruelty is badly or well used. Cruelties may be called well used — if of evil one may speak well at all — when they are committed all at once, out of the need to make yourself secure, and then are not kept up, but turned to the good of your subjects. They are badly used when, few though they may be at the start, they grow with time instead of dying away. Those who take the first course can, with God's help or man's, find some way to soften their rule, as Agathocles did. Those who take the second cannot possibly keep their footing.

From this it is to be noted that in seizing a state, a man should reckon up all the injuries he must inflict, and do them all at one stroke, so as not to be repeating them day after day; for then, by not unsettling men, he can reassure them and win them over with benefits. Whoever does otherwise, whether out of timidity or bad advice, must always keep the knife in his hand; he can never rely on his subjects, nor they trust themselves to him, because of the fresh and ceaseless wrongs he does them. For injuries should be done all at once, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits should be handed out little by little, so that their flavor lasts longer.

And above all, a prince should live among his people in such a way that no turn of events, good or bad, can force him to change course. For if the need comes upon you in troubled times, you are too late for harsh measures; and any kindness you show will do you no good, since it will be seen as wrung out of you, and no one will thank you for it.

sections.label: Chapter IX
sections.title: Concerning a Civil Principality

segments.text: Now for the other way up. A leading citizen becomes the prince of his country not by crime, nor by any unbearable show of force, but by the favor of his fellow citizens. This may be called a civil principality, and reaching it takes neither great skill nor great luck, but rather a shrewdness that knows its moment. Such a principality is won either by the favor of the people or by the favor of the nobles. For in every city these two opposed parties are found, and the source of the split is this: the people do not want to be commanded or oppressed by the nobles, and the nobles want to command and oppress the people. Out of these two contrary appetites one of three things comes about in a city — a principality, a free government, or anarchy.

Whether the principality comes from the people or from the nobles depends on which of them gets the opening. When the nobles see they cannot hold out against the people, they begin to talk up the standing of one of their own and make him prince, so that under his cover they can satisfy their own ambitions. The people, when they find they cannot resist the nobles, likewise talk up the standing of one of their own and make him prince, to have his authority for their shield. A man who reaches power with the help of the nobles holds it with more difficulty than one who reaches it by the help of the people, because he finds himself surrounded by many who count themselves his equals, and so he can neither command them nor manage them as he likes. But the man who reaches power by the people's favor stands there alone, with no one around him, or next to no one, unwilling to obey.

Beyond that, you cannot in fairness, and without wronging others, satisfy the nobles — but you can satisfy the people, because their aim is more honest than the nobles': the nobles want to oppress, the people want only not to be oppressed. And there is this too: a prince can never make himself safe against a hostile people, since they are too many, whereas against the nobles he can, since they are few. The worst a prince has to fear from a hostile people is to be abandoned by them; but from hostile nobles he has to fear not only abandonment but their turning against him — for being shrewder and more far-sighted in these matters, they always move in time to save themselves, and to court the favor of the man they expect to win. And there is more: a prince is forced to go on living always with the same people, but he can do well enough without the same nobles, since he can make them and unmake them day by day, granting and stripping their standing whenever he pleases.

To make this point clearer: the nobles are to be looked at chiefly in two ways. Either they so bind themselves to your fortune that their whole course is tied to yours, or they do not. Those who bind themselves to you, and are not greedy, should be honored and loved. Those who do not bind themselves split into two kinds. Some hold back out of timidity, a natural want of nerve; these you should put to use, especially the ones who give good counsel, since in good times they bring you honor and in bad times you have nothing to fear from them. But those who hold off out of calculation, for their own ambitious ends, are showing that they think more of themselves than of you; and a prince should be on his guard against these and fear them as if they were declared enemies, because when things turn against him they will always help to bring him down.

So a man who becomes prince by the favor of the people should keep them friendly, which is easily done, since all they ask is not to be oppressed. But a man who becomes prince by the favor of the nobles, against the people, should before anything else work to win the people over to himself — which is also easily done, if he takes them under his protection. For when men receive good from someone they had braced for harm, they bind themselves to their benefactor all the more tightly; and so the people will turn more devoted to him than if he had been raised to power by their own favor in the first place. A prince can win the people in many ways, but since these change with the circumstances no fixed rule can be laid down, so I leave them aside. The conclusion stands: a prince must have the people friendly, or in hard times he has nothing to fall back on.

Nabis, prince of the Spartans, withstood the assault of all Greece and of a Roman army flush with victory, and against them defended his country and his state; and to ride out that danger he had only to make himself secure against a few — though that would not have been enough had the people been against him. And let no one throw the worn-out proverb at this opinion of mine, that "he who builds on the people builds on mud." That holds when a private citizen makes the people his foundation and lets himself believe they will come to his rescue when his enemies or the magistrates bear down on him — in which case he will often find himself deceived, as the Gracchi were in Rome and Messer Giorgio Scali in Florence. But take a prince who has established himself as I have described, who can command, who is a man of nerve, not thrown by adversity, who does not fall short in the other qualities, and who by his resolve and his energy keeps the whole people heartened — such a prince will never be deceived by them, and will be shown to have laid his foundations well.

These principalities are most in danger when they are passing from the civil to the absolute order of rule. For such princes govern either in person or through magistrates. In the second case their position is weaker and less secure, since it rests entirely on the goodwill of those citizens raised to office, who in troubled times can wreck the government with great ease, whether by scheming or by open defiance. And in the thick of such upheavals the prince has no chance to seize absolute authority, because the citizens and subjects, used to taking their orders from the magistrates, are in no mood amid the confusion to take them from him; and in doubtful times he will always be short of men he can trust. A prince of this kind cannot count on what he sees in quiet times, when the citizens need the state — for then they all rush to agree with him, all make promises, and with death far off all swear to die for him; but when trouble comes, when the state has need of its citizens, then he finds very few. And the test is the more dangerous because it can be run only once. So a wise prince must contrive things in such a way that his citizens, in every kind of circumstance whatever, always have need of the state and of him; and then they will always be faithful to him.

sections.label: Chapter X
sections.title: How the Strength of All Principalities Should Be Measured

segments.text: There is one more point to weigh when examining the character of these principalities: whether a prince has power enough to stand on his own at need, or whether he must always lean on the help of others. To make this plain, I count as able to stand on their own those who, by abundance of men or money, can raise an army strong enough to take the field against anyone who comes to attack them; and I count as always needing others those who cannot face the enemy in the open but are forced to shelter behind their walls and defend those. The first case I have already discussed, and will return to as occasion requires. To those in the second case there is nothing to say except to urge them to provision and fortify their towns, and never on any account to defend the open country. Whoever fortifies his town well, and has handled his subjects' affairs as I described above and will describe again, will never be attacked without great caution; for men are always loath to take on enterprises that look difficult, and there is no easy prize in attacking a prince whose town is well fortified and who is not hated by his people.

The cities of Germany are wholly free; they own little of the country around them, and they obey the emperor only when it suits them, fearing neither him nor any other power they have near them, because they are fortified in such a way that everyone reckons the taking of them by assault would be slow and hard. They all have proper ditches and walls; they have artillery enough; and they always keep stored in public depots enough to eat, drink, and burn for a year. On top of this, to keep the common people content without cost to the state, they always have the means to set them to work for a year at the labors that are the life and strength of the city, the trades by which the people live. They hold military exercises in honor besides, and have many ordinances to keep them up.

So a prince who has a strong city and has not made himself hated cannot be attacked; and if anyone should attack him, he will be driven off in disgrace, for the affairs of this world shift so much that it is all but impossible for a man to keep an army idle in the field for a whole year, laying siege. And should someone object that, if the people have property outside the walls and see it burned, they will lose patience, and the long siege and their own self-interest will make them forget their prince — to this I answer that a powerful and spirited prince will master every such difficulty: now giving his subjects hope that the trouble will not last long, now turning their minds to fear of the enemy's cruelty, now dealing shrewdly with those who seem too bold.

Besides, the enemy will naturally burn and lay waste the country the moment he arrives, while the people's spirits are still hot and set on the defense; and so the prince has all the less reason to hesitate, because a few days on, when those spirits have cooled, the damage is already done, the harm is already taken, and there is no remedy left. By then the people only bind themselves more closely to their prince, judging that he stands in their debt now that their houses have been burned and their lands ruined in his defense. For it is the nature of men to feel as much bound by the good they do as by the good they receive. So weigh it all up, and a wise prince will find it no hard thing to keep his citizens' spirits firm through a siege from first to last, so long as he does not fail to feed them and to defend them.

sections.label: Chapter XI
sections.title: Concerning Ecclesiastical Principalities

segments.text: It remains only to speak of ecclesiastical principalities. With these, all the difficulty lies in getting hold of them, for they are won either by skill or by fortune, and held by neither. They are sustained instead by the ancient institutions of religion, which are so powerful, and of such a kind, that they keep their princes in power no matter how those princes act or live. These princes alone have states and do not defend them; they have subjects and do not govern them; and yet their states, undefended, are not taken from them, and their subjects, ungoverned, do not mind, and have neither the wish nor the means to break away. Such principalities alone are secure and content. But since they are upheld by powers the human mind cannot reach, I will say no more about them: being exalted and maintained by God, it would be the act of a presumptuous and rash man to discuss them.

Still, someone might ask how it comes about that the Church has grown so great in temporal power. Before Alexander, the Italian powers — and not just those properly called powers, but every baron and lord, down to the very smallest — counted that temporal power for very little; yet now a king of France trembles before it, and it has been able to drive him out of Italy and to ruin the Venetians. The thing may be plain enough, but I think it worth recalling to mind.

Before Charles, King of France, came down into Italy, this country lay under the dominion of the Pope, the Venetians, the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and the Florentines. These powers had two chief anxieties: first, that no foreigner should enter Italy under arms; second, that none of their own number should seize more territory. The two watched most closely were the Pope and the Venetians. To hold the Venetians in check, all the others had to combine, as they did in the defense of Ferrara; and to keep the Pope down, they made use of the barons of Rome, who, split into two factions, the Orsini and the Colonna, always had some pretext for disorder, and, standing with arms in hand under the very eyes of the pontiff, kept the papacy weak and helpless. And though now and again a bold pope would arise, a Sixtus for instance, neither his fortune nor his wisdom could ever rid him of these troubles. The short life of a pope was a cause of weakness too: in the ten years that is a pope's average reign, he could barely beat down one of the factions, and if, say, one pope had nearly destroyed the Colonna, another would come up hostile to the Orsini, who would revive the Colonna again — and yet would not live long enough to crush the Orsini in his turn. This is why the temporal power of the pope counted for so little in Italy.

Then came Alexander VI, who, of all the popes there have ever been, showed how far a pope could prevail with money and with arms. Using Duke Valentino as his instrument, and seizing on the entry of the French, he brought about all those things I described above in recounting the duke's actions. And although his aim was not to make the Church great but the duke, what he did told all the same to the Church's greatness — for after his death and the duke's ruin, the Church fell heir to all his labors.

Pope Julius came next, and found the Church strong: master of all the Romagna, with the barons of Rome reduced to impotence and their factions wiped out by Alexander's chastisements, and with the way open, as never before Alexander's time, to heap up money. Julius not only carried on what he found but improved upon it. He set out to take Bologna, to ruin the Venetians, and to drive the French out of Italy; and in all these enterprises he succeeded, and to his greater credit, since he did everything to strengthen the Church and no private man. He kept the Orsini and Colonna factions within the bounds in which he found them; and though there was still some appetite for trouble among them, two things held firm. One was the greatness of the Church, with which he overawed them; the other was his refusal to let them have cardinals of their own, for cardinals are the root of the disorders among them. Whenever these factions have their cardinals, they will not stay quiet for long, since cardinals foster the factions in Rome and outside it, and the barons are forced to back them — and so out of the ambitions of prelates spring the quarrels and tumults of the barons. For these reasons His Holiness Pope Leo has found the papacy at the height of its power; and it is to be hoped that, if his predecessors made it great by arms, he will make it greater still, and more revered, by his goodness and his countless other virtues.

sections.label: Chapter XII
sections.title: How Many Kinds of Soldiery There Are, and Concerning Mercenaries

segments.text: Having dealt one by one with the kinds of principality I set out at the start to examine, and having weighed in some measure why one fares well and another badly, and shown the methods by which men have sought to win them and to hold them, it remains for me to discuss in general the means of attack and defense that belong to each.

We have seen already how necessary it is for a prince to have his foundations well laid; otherwise he is bound to come to ruin. The chief foundations of every state — new, old, or mixed — are good laws and good arms. And since there cannot be good laws where there are not good arms, and where there are good arms there are bound to be good laws, I will set the laws aside and speak of the arms.

I say, then, that the arms with which a prince defends his state are either his own, or mercenary, or auxiliary, or a mixture of these. Mercenary and auxiliary arms are useless and dangerous; and any man who rests his state on mercenaries will never stand firm or safe. For they are disunited, ambitious, undisciplined, and faithless; brave among friends, cowardly among enemies; with no fear of God and no good faith toward men. Ruin is put off only for as long as the assault is put off; in peace you are robbed by them, in war by the enemy. The reason is that they have no love and no motive to keep the field beyond their scrap of pay, which is not enough to make them willing to die for you. They are glad to be your soldiers while you wage no war, but when war comes they either bolt or run from the foe. I should have little trouble proving this, for the ruin of Italy has been caused by nothing but her resting, for so many years, all her hopes on mercenaries. They did, it is true, make some showing for a time and looked brave enough among themselves; but when the foreigners came they showed what they were. So it was that Charles, King of France, was let seize Italy with chalk in hand. The man who said our sins were the cause of it spoke the truth — only they were not the sins he had in mind, but the ones I have described; and since they were the sins of princes, the princes too have paid the penalty.

I want to show further how wretched these arms are. The mercenary captains are either able men or they are not. If they are, you cannot trust them, because they will always be reaching for their own greatness, either by crushing you, their own master, or by crushing others against your will. And if the captain is no soldier, he ruins you in the ordinary way.

And if it is objected that any man under arms, mercenary or not, will do the same, I answer this: arms have to be wielded either by a prince or by a republic. The prince ought to go in person and serve as his own captain. The republic must send its own citizens; and when it sends one who does not prove himself, it should recall him, and when it sends a worthy one, it should bind him by the laws so that he cannot overstep his command. Experience shows that princes who stand alone, and republics under their own arms, make the greatest headway, while mercenary arms do nothing but harm; and a republic armed with its own arms is far harder to bring under the rule of one of its citizens than a republic armed with foreign arms. Rome and Sparta stood for ages armed and free. The Swiss are fully armed and entirely free.

For an example of mercenaries in ancient times, take the Carthaginians, who were nearly overthrown by their own hired soldiers after the first war with Rome, even though the Carthaginians had men of their own for captains. After the death of Epaminondas, the Thebans made Philip of Macedon captain of their army, and after the victory he stripped them of their freedom.

When Duke Filippo died, the Milanese hired Francesco Sforza against the Venetians; and once he had beaten the enemy at Caravaggio, he joined with them to crush the Milanese, his own employers. His father, the elder Sforza, in the pay of Queen Giovanna of Naples, abandoned her without warning, so that to save her kingdom she was forced to throw herself into the arms of the King of Aragon. And if it is said that the Venetians and Florentines did once enlarge their dominions with such arms, and yet their captains did not make themselves princes but defended them faithfully, I answer that the Florentines in this were favored by luck. Of the able captains they might have had reason to fear, some did not win their wars, some met opposition, and others turned their ambition elsewhere. One who did not win was Giovanni Acuto — Sir John Hawkwood — and since he did not win, his loyalty was never put to the test; but everyone will admit that, had he won, the Florentines would have lain at his mercy. Sforza always had the Bracceschi against him, so the two watched each other in check: Francesco turned his ambition toward Lombardy, Braccio against the Church and the kingdom of Naples. But let us come to what happened only a little while ago. The Florentines made Paolo Vitelli their captain, a most shrewd man who had risen from private life to the highest renown. Had he taken Pisa, no one can deny the Florentines would have been bound to keep on his good side, for if he had gone over to their enemies they would have had no way to resist him, and if they held on to him they would have had to obey him. As for the Venetians, look at their record and you will see they acted safely and gloriously so long as they sent their own men to war — when, with their armed gentlemen and commoners, they fought bravely. This was before they turned to campaigns on land; once they began fighting on land, they abandoned that virtue and fell in with the custom of Italy. In the early stage of their expansion on land, having little territory and a great reputation, they had not much to fear from their captains. But as they expanded, under Carmagnola, they got a taste of their mistake. They had found him a most able commander — under him they had beaten the Duke of Milan — yet they also saw how lukewarm he had grown in the war, and they judged they would win no more under him. They were unwilling to let him go, and unable to, for fear of losing back what they had gained; so, to make themselves safe, they were driven to murder him. After him they had for captains Bartolomeo da Bergamo, Roberto da San Severino, the Count of Pitigliano, and the like — men under whom they had loss to dread and no gain to hope for, as duly happened later at Vailà, where in a single battle they lost what it had cost them eight hundred years of toil to win. For from such arms come only conquests that are slow, late, and slight, but losses that are sudden and staggering.

And since these examples have brought me to Italy, which has been ruled for so many years by mercenaries, I want to take them up more seriously, so that, having traced their rise and progress, one may be better placed to set them right. You must understand that in recent times the empire has come to be cast off in Italy, that the Pope has gained more temporal power, and that Italy has been carved up into more states. The reason is that many of the great cities took up arms against their own nobles, who, once favored by the emperor, had been oppressing them, while the Church backed the cities to build up its own temporal authority; and in many others, private citizens became princes. So Italy fell largely into the hands of the Church and of republics; and since the Church is made up of priests and the republic of citizens unused to arms, both began to hire foreigners.

The first to give this kind of soldiery a name was Alberigo da Conio, the Romagnol. Out of his school came, among others, Braccio and Sforza, who in their day were the arbiters of Italy. After them came all the other captains who down to our own time have directed the arms of Italy; and the upshot of all their prowess has been that she has been overrun by Charles, plundered by Louis, ravaged by Ferdinand, and disgraced by the Swiss. The first principle these captains followed was to take all credit from the infantry, to raise their own. They did this because, living on their pay and holding no territory of their own, they could not keep many men, and a handful of foot soldiers gave them no standing; so they took to cavalry, of which a manageable number kept them maintained and honored. Things came to such a pass that in an army of twenty thousand men there were not two thousand on foot. Beyond this, they had used every device to spare themselves and their soldiers hardship and danger, not killing one another in the fray but taking prisoners and releasing them without ransom. They would not attack towns by night, nor would the garrisons of the towns attack their camps by night; they ringed their camp with neither stockade nor ditch; they did not take the field in winter. All this their military rules allowed, and all of it was contrived, as I have said, to dodge effort and danger — and so they have led Italy into slavery and contempt.

sections.label: Chapter XIII
sections.title: Concerning Auxiliaries, Mixed Soldiery, and One's Own

segments.text: Auxiliaries are the other useless kind of arms. You take them on when you call in some power to come with its own forces to aid and defend you, as Pope Julius did not long ago: having had poor proof of his mercenaries in the campaign against Ferrara, he turned to auxiliaries and struck a bargain with Ferdinand, King of Spain, for help in men and arms. Such arms may be useful and good in themselves, but for the man who calls them in they are always a danger. For if you lose, you are undone; and if you win, you are their prisoner.

Ancient history is full of examples, but I will not pass over this recent one of Pope Julius II, whose recklessness could not be plainer. In his eagerness to get Ferrara, he threw himself wholly into the hands of a foreigner. But his good luck brought on a third turn of events, so that he did not reap the fruit of his rash choice. For when his auxiliaries were routed at Ravenna, and the Swiss then rose up and drove out the victors — against all expectation, his and everyone else's — it came about that he fell prisoner neither to his enemies, who had fled, nor to his auxiliaries, since he had won by other arms than theirs.
The Florentines, entirely without arms of their own, sent ten thousand Frenchmen to take Pisa, and by doing so ran more danger than at any other point in all their troubles.

The Emperor of Constantinople, to stand against his neighbors, sent ten thousand Turks into Greece, who, once the war was over, would not leave; and that was the beginning of the enslavement of Greece to the infidels.

So let the man who has no wish to conquer make use of these arms, for they are far more hazardous than mercenaries. With auxiliaries the ruin is ready-made: they are all united, and all trained to obey someone else. With mercenaries, even after they have won, more time and a better opening are needed before they can do you harm, since they are not all of one body, and they are found and paid by you — and a man you have set at their head cannot, all at once, take on enough authority to injure you. In short, with mercenaries the danger is their cowardice; with auxiliaries, their courage. So the wise prince has always shunned these arms and turned to his own, choosing rather to lose with his own men than to win with the others, since he counts no true victory one that is won with the arms of others.

I will never hold back from citing Cesare Borgia and what he did. This duke entered the Romagna with auxiliaries, bringing nothing but French soldiers, and with them he took Imola and Forlì. But when those forces came to seem unreliable to him, he turned to mercenaries, judging them less of a risk, and hired the Orsini and the Vitelli. Then, finding these doubtful, faithless, and dangerous as he handled them, he destroyed them and fell back on his own men. And the difference between one kind of force and the other is easily seen if you weigh how the duke's standing differed when he had only the French, when he had the Orsini and Vitelli, and when he relied on his own soldiers and his own strength: his reputation always rose, and he was never held in higher esteem than when everyone saw that he was complete master of his own forces.

I meant to keep to Italian and recent examples, but I will not leave out Hiero of Syracuse, since he is one of those I named earlier. This man, as I have said, was made head of the army by the Syracusans, and soon found that mercenary soldiery — made up the way our Italian condottieri are — was good for nothing. Judging that he could neither keep them nor safely let them go, he had them all cut to pieces, and afterward made war with his own forces and not with hired men.

I want to call to mind, too, an instance from the Old Testament that bears on this. When David offered himself to Saul to fight Goliath, the Philistine champion, Saul, to give him heart, armed him with his own armor. But David, once he had it on his back, refused it, saying he could make no use of it, and that he would rather meet the enemy with his sling and his knife. In short, another man's armor either slips off your back, or weighs you down, or binds you fast.

Charles the Seventh, father of King Louis the Eleventh, having by good luck and skill freed France from the English, saw the necessity of arming himself with forces of his own, and set up in his kingdom ordinances for men-at-arms and infantry. Afterward his son, King Louis, did away with the infantry and began hiring the Swiss — a blunder that, followed by others, is now plainly a source of peril to that kingdom. For by raising the standing of the Swiss he has wholly lowered the worth of his own arms: he scrapped the infantry altogether, and tied his men-at-arms to others, since, being so used to fighting alongside the Swiss, they no longer think they can win without them. And so the French cannot hold their ground against the Swiss, and without the Swiss they come off badly against anyone else. The armies of France have thus become mixed, part mercenary and part their own — a combination far better than mercenaries alone or auxiliaries alone, but far worse than forces wholly one's own. And this example proves it: France would be unconquerable if the ordinance of Charles had been built upon and kept up.

But man's scant wisdom, going into a thing that looks well at first, cannot make out the poison hidden in it — as I said before of wasting fevers. So the man who rules a principality and cannot recognize troubles until they are upon him is not truly wise; and this insight is given to few. And if you trace the first disaster of the Roman Empire, you will find it began precisely with the hiring of the Goths; for from that point the vigor of the Roman Empire started to fail, and all the prowess that had built it up drained away to others.

I conclude, then, that no principality is secure without its own arms — on the contrary, it rests wholly on fortune, having no prowess of its own to defend it in adversity. It has always been the opinion and judgment of wise men that nothing is so weak and unstable as a reputation for power that is not founded on a power of one's own. And one's own arms are those made up of subjects, citizens, or your own dependents; all the rest are mercenary or auxiliary. The way to make ready arms of one's own will be easily found if you reflect on the rules I have set down, and consider how Philip, the father of Alexander the Great, and many republics and princes have armed and organized themselves — to which rules I wholly commit myself.

sections.label: Chapter XIV
sections.title: A Prince's Duty Concerning Military Affairs

segments.text: A prince should have no other aim or thought, nor take up anything else for his study, but war and its organization and discipline; for this is the one art expected of a man who rules. It is of such force that it not only keeps in power those born princes, but often raises men from private station to that rank. And the reverse is just as plainly seen: when princes have given more thought to their comfort than to arms, they have lost their states. The first cause of losing a state is neglecting this art; and the thing that wins you one is being its master. Francesco Sforza, because he was armed, rose from a private man to Duke of Milan; his sons, because they shirked the hardships of arms, sank from dukes to private men. For among the other evils that being unarmed brings you, it makes you despised — and contempt is one of those disgraces a prince must guard himself against, as I will show further on. Between an armed man and an unarmed one there is no proportion whatever; it stands to no reason that the armed man should willingly obey the unarmed, or that the unarmed should be safe among armed servants. There is scorn on the one side and suspicion on the other, and the two can never work well together. So a prince who knows nothing of war, on top of the other misfortunes already named, cannot be respected by his soldiers, nor can he trust them. He should therefore never let this subject of war out of his thoughts, and in peace he should train at it harder than in war itself. This he can do in two ways: by action and by study.

As for action, above all he should keep his men well organized and drilled, and never stop hunting, by which he hardens his body to hardship and at the same time learns the lie of the land — how the mountains rise, how the valleys open out, how the plains lie — and comes to understand the nature of rivers and marshes, giving all of this his closest attention. This knowledge is useful two ways. First, he comes to know his own country, and is the better able to defend it. Then, through the knowledge and observation he has of one place, he grasps any other he may need to study with ease; for the hills, valleys, plains, rivers, and marshes of Tuscany, say, have a certain likeness to those of other regions, so that from knowing the terrain of one country one passes easily to knowing others. The prince who lacks this skill lacks the first thing a commander needs, for it is what teaches him to surprise the enemy, choose his ground, lead his army, draw up the line of battle, and lay siege to towns to his advantage.

Philopoemen, prince of the Achaeans, among the other praises writers have heaped on him, is commended for this: that in time of peace he thought of nothing but the conduct of war. When he was out in the country with friends he would often stop and reason with them — "If the enemy were on that hill, and we stood here with our army, which of us would have the advantage? How could we advance on him in good order? If we wanted to retreat, how should we go about it? If he retreated, how should we give chase?" And as they went along he would put to them every contingency that can befall an army; he would hear their view and give his own, backing it with reasons. So from this constant turning of cases over, no situation could ever arise in war that he had not already met and could not handle.

But as for the exercise of the mind, the prince should read histories, and there study the deeds of great men: see how they bore themselves in their wars, examine the causes of their victories and defeats, so as to avoid the one and copy the other. Above all he should do as some great man has done before him, who took as his model one who had been praised and held glorious before his own time, and kept that man's bearing and conduct always before him — as it is said Alexander the Great imitated Achilles, Caesar imitated Alexander, and Scipio imitated Cyrus. And anyone who reads the life of Cyrus written by Xenophon will see, in the life of Scipio, how much that imitation made his glory, and how closely in self-command, courtesy, humanity, and generosity Scipio kept to the things Xenophon wrote of Cyrus. A wise prince should hold to ways like these, and never sit idle in times of peace, but make capital of them by his own diligence, so that he may draw on it in adversity — so that when fortune turns, it finds him ready to withstand her.

sections.label: Chapter XV
sections.title: Concerning Things for Which Men, and Especially Princes, Are Praised or Blamed

segments.text: It remains now to see how a prince ought to conduct himself toward his subjects and his friends. And since I know that many have written on this, I am afraid that in writing of it again I shall be thought presumptuous, the more so because I depart, in discussing it, from the methods of the others. But as my intention is to write something useful to anyone who grasps it, it has seemed to me more to the point to go after the effectual truth of the matter than the imagination of it. For many have pictured republics and principalities that were never seen or known to exist in fact; because how one lives is so far removed from how one ought to live, that the man who lets go of what is done for what ought to be done sooner learns his ruin than his preservation. For a man who sets out to act the good man in every way must come to grief among so many who are not good.

And so a prince who means to hold his own must learn how not to be good, and to use this or not use it according to necessity.
